commonMistakes: Solving the wrong problem by skipping clarification.
Testing only the happy path and missing empty input or the last-element flush.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A reliable process is: restate the problem and confirm it with examples, clarify the five things that change solutions most (sorted or not, duplicates, negatives, empty or missing answers, mutability), work a small example by hand to find the pattern, state a brute force and its complexity, then optimise, code while explaining each step, and test in three layers: the given examples, edge cases (empty, single, identical, sorted, reverse), and one adversarial case aimed at your solution's weak point. State time and space complexity without being asked. If stuck for more than a few minutes, say so and ask for a hint; if time runs short, finish a working brute force rather than a half-finished optimal solution.
followUps: What do you do if you spot a better approach halfway through coding?
How do you handle a follow-up that breaks your solution?
How do you practise this process?
interviewQuestions.question: Walk through your process for a coding problem you have never seen before.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Restate, clarify, hand-work an example, brute force, optimise, code aloud, test in three layers, state complexity, and anticipate follow-ups.
tips: Timebox: roughly 5 minutes clarifying, 15 to 20 coding, the rest testing and follow-ups.
Name the follow-up ladder: space, constraints, scale, output.
interviewQuestions.title: Interview problem-solving process

commonMistakes: Applying a sliding window where the invariant is not monotone.
Claiming a greedy solution without any safety argument.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The constraint change decides the new pattern. Adding negative numbers breaks a sliding window for sum constraints, because shrinking can increase the sum, so switch to prefix sums with a map, or a monotonic deque for the shortest subarray variant. Requiring O(1) space rules out a HashMap, so switch to sorting plus two pointers if indices are not needed, or to an in-place technique. Asking for all solutions instead of one moves a problem from search to enumeration, often backtracking, and asking for a count moves it towards DP. The skill interviewers test here is not knowing every variant, but reasoning from why the original pattern worked and which of its preconditions the new constraint violates.
followUps: What if the input becomes a stream that does not fit in memory?
What if you need the count of solutions, not the solutions themselves?
What if duplicates are now allowed?
interviewQuestions.question: Your solution works, but the interviewer changes a constraint. How do you adapt?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Identify which precondition of your pattern the new constraint violates, then switch to the pattern whose preconditions still hold, and re-state the new complexity.
tips: Name the broken precondition explicitly, for example monotonicity for sliding windows.
Offer the replacement pattern, not just a patch.
interviewQuestions.title: Adapting to changed constraints

commonMistakes: Saying closures copy variables instead of capturing them by reference.
Confusing closures with scope in general, or with the module pattern specifically.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A closure is a function combined with the lexical environment where it was created. When the outer function returns, variables it declared would normally be discarded, but if an inner function still references them, the environment stays alive. This is how callbacks retain state, how factory functions create private state, and how event handlers remember the data they were created with. Each call to the outer function creates a fresh environment, so closures created by different calls do not share state.
followUps: How would you use a closure to create private state?
What is the classic var-in-a-loop closure bug, and how does let fix it?
interviewQuestions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give an example.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A function that retains access to variables from the scope where it was created, even after the outer function has returned.
tips: Give a concrete example such as a counter factory, and explain that each call creates a fresh captured environment.
Mention a real use: callbacks, private state, or debouncing.
interviewQuestions.title: Closures

commonMistakes: Saying var is block-scoped, or that let is not hoisted at all (it is hoisted but in the temporal dead zone).
Claiming hoisting means the assignment moves, rather than the declaration.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: var is function-scoped and hoisted with an initial value of undefined, so reading it before its line gives undefined rather than an error. let and const are block-scoped and also hoisted, but they live in the temporal dead zone between the start of the block and their declaration, so reading them early throws a ReferenceError. Function declarations are hoisted fully and can be called before their line; function expressions assigned to variables follow the rules of the variable kind. Modern code prefers const by default and let for reassignment, avoiding var entirely.
followUps: What is the temporal dead zone?
Why does a var loop variable break setTimeout callbacks, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.question: Explain hoisting and the difference between var, let, and const.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Declarations are processed before execution: var is function-scoped and initialised to undefined, while let and const are block-scoped and throw if used before declaration.
tips: Draw the temporal dead zone explicitly; interviewers check whether you know let is hoisted too.
Give the loop-with-setTimeout example as the practical consequence.
interviewQuestions.title: Hoisting, var, let, const

commonMistakes: Saying the event loop is what makes JavaScript multithreaded.
Forgetting that microtasks drain fully before the next macrotask.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: JavaScript executes on a single thread: synchronous code runs to completion on the call stack. When the stack empties, the event loop takes work from task queues. Microtasks — promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks — drain completely before the next macrotask, which includes timers, I/O callbacks, and rendering steps. That is why a resolved promise callback runs before a setTimeout with delay zero, even if the timer was scheduled first. Long synchronous work blocks everything, including rendering and user input, because nothing else can run until the stack empties.
followUps: Why does a long loop freeze the page?
How do web workers fit into this picture?
interviewQuestions.question: How does the JavaScript event loop work, and why does a promise callback run before setTimeout(..., 0)?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The call stack runs first, then all queued microtasks drain, and only then does the next macrotask (such as a timer) run.
tips: Walk through a short code example step by step rather than reciting definitions.
Name the queues explicitly: microtask queue versus macrotask queue.
interviewQuestions.title: The event loop

commonMistakes: Forgetting to check response.ok and treating every resolved fetch as success.
Not handling rejection, leaving unhandled rejections.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: fetch returns a promise that rejects only on network failure, not on HTTP error statuses. A 404 or 500 response resolves normally, so code must check response.ok or response.status and throw or handle accordingly. For robust code, start independent requests together and await them with Promise.all, wrap awaits in try/catch, and pass an AbortSignal from an AbortController when the request should be cancellable — for example when a component unmounts or the user types a new query. Distinguish abort errors from real failures so cancellations do not show error messages.
followUps: How do you cancel a fetch?
When would you use Promise.allSettled instead of Promise.all?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you fetch data in JavaScript, and what are the common pitfalls?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use fetch with async/await, check response.ok because HTTP errors still resolve, handle rejections, and cancel with AbortController when the request becomes stale.
tips: Always mention response.ok — interviewers specifically look for it.
Bring up stale responses and cancellation for a stronger answer.
interviewQuestions.title: Fetching data with fetch

commonMistakes: Confusing event.target with event.currentTarget.
Calling stopPropagation when preventDefault was meant, or vice versa.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An event travels in three phases: capturing from the window down to the target, at the target, then bubbling back up. Listeners default to the bubbling phase. Event delegation exploits bubbling: a single listener on a parent inspects event.target to decide which child was involved, which is cheaper than a listener per child and works for elements added later. preventDefault stops the browser's default action, such as following a link or submitting a form; stopPropagation stops the event travelling further. They are independent and are often confused.
followUps: How would you implement delegation for a list with delete buttons?
What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
interviewQuestions.question: Explain event bubbling and event delegation. When would you use delegation?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Events bubble from the target up through ancestors, so one parent listener can handle many children by checking event.target.
tips: Give a concrete example: a todo list with delete buttons, including dynamically added items.
State the target versus currentTarget distinction unprompted.
interviewQuestions.title: Event bubbling and delegation

commonMistakes: Saying TypeScript adds runtime type checking.
Using any to silence errors instead of fixing the underlying mismatch.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: TypeScript adds a static type layer that is checked at compile time and then erased, so the shipped code is plain JavaScript with no runtime type checks. That is why runtime validation of external data is still necessary. any opts out of checking and lets errors through to runtime, while unknown is the safe alternative: it accepts any value but requires narrowing before use. Strict mode, especially strictNullChecks, is what makes the system genuinely useful, because without it null and undefined are assignable to everything.
followUps: When is any acceptable, and when should you use unknown instead?
How do you validate API data at runtime if types are erased?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between any and unknown in TypeScript?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: any disables type checking; unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow it before use.
tips: Mention type erasure: types never reach runtime, which is why unknown plus a runtime check is the safe pattern.
Say when you would actually use each one.
interviewQuestions.title: any versus unknown

commonMistakes: Saying interfaces and type aliases are interchangeable in all cases — aliases can name unions and tuples, interfaces can merge and extend.
Over-generifying a helper used in exactly one place.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A generic function or type declares type parameters, such as T, that callers supply implicitly through inference or explicitly. This preserves the relationship between inputs and outputs: a generic identity or first-element helper returns the caller's type, whereas an any-based version discards that information. Constraints with extends restrict what a type argument may be, so the implementation can safely use required properties. keyof combined with generics gives type-safe property access, and utility types such as Partial, Pick, and Omit replace duplicated hand-written variants.
followUps: How do you write a generic function that safely reads a property by key?
When is a generic the wrong tool, and what would you use instead?
interviewQuestions.question: What are generics in TypeScript, and why are they better than any for reusable helpers?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Generics parameterise a function or type by type, so one implementation serves many types while preserving type information at each call site.
tips: Write a tiny example on the board, such as first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined.
Mention constraints and keyof to show depth beyond the basic definition.
interviewQuestions.title: TypeScript generics

commonMistakes: Typing children as JSX.Element, which rejects text and arrays.
Forgetting the element generic on event types, losing currentTarget properties.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Props are a plain object type, and children should be typed ReactNode, which covers elements, strings, numbers, fragments, arrays, and null — far wider than JSX.Element. Events use synthetic types parameterised by element, such as React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, which determines what currentTarget offers. useState infers its type from the initial value, so useState<User | null>(null) needs an explicit generic when the initial value is narrower than the real state. DOM refs start as null and must be checked. Generic components infer their type parameter from props at each use site, keeping reusable UI type-safe.
followUps: Why is React.FC discouraged in modern codebases?
How would you type a reducer's actions in a component?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you type React components, props, and events in TypeScript?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Props as an object type, children as ReactNode, events as React synthetic types parameterised by element, and explicit generics where inference would be too narrow.
tips: Name ReactNode explicitly and explain why JSX.Element is too narrow.
Give the useState<User | null>(null) example.
interviewQuestions.title: Typing React with TypeScript

commonMistakes: Saying hooks can be conditional as long as the condition is stable — they cannot, because order must be identical on every render.
Omitting dependencies and debugging stale values instead of fixing the dependency array.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: React tracks hooks by call order across renders, which is why they must be called unconditionally at the top level of a component or custom hook. A hook inside a condition or loop would shift the order of every later hook and attach state to the wrong hook. useState holds a value across renders and triggers re-renders when changed; useRef holds a mutable value without triggering renders; useEffect runs after commit and its cleanup runs before the next effect run and on unmount. Custom hooks reuse logic, not state — each component calling the hook gets its own independent state.
followUps: What is a stale closure, and how do missing effect dependencies cause one?
Why do effects run twice in React 18 Strict Mode development?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the rules of hooks, and why do they exist?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level, because React identifies them by call order across renders.
tips: Explain the mechanism (call order), not just the rule — that is what interviewers reward.
Mention the exhaustive-deps lint rule as the practical enforcement.
interviewQuestions.title: Rules of hooks

commonMistakes: Putting fetched data in plain useState and re-implementing caching badly.
Putting everything in one context and re-rendering the whole app on every change.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start with local state and lift it only when another component needs it. useReducer centralises complex, interrelated updates as explicit actions, which is easier to test and reason about than scattered setters. Context passes values down without prop drilling but is not a state manager: it has no update mechanism and no selectors, so every consumer re-renders when the value changes. Fetched data is server state — a cache with loading, error, freshness, and invalidation concerns — and belongs in a server-state library rather than hand-rolled useEffect fetching. External stores with selectors suit frequently changing shared client state. Shareable state such as filters belongs in the URL.
followUps: How would you design state for a shopping cart versus a dashboard?
When would you choose Redux Toolkit over context?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide where state should live in a React application?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Local by default; lift when shared, reduce when transitions are complex, context for rarely changing shared values, and a dedicated library for server state.
tips: Frame the answer by kind of state: local, shared, server, URL — not by library name.
Mention context's re-render behaviour explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: State design in React

commonMistakes: Wrapping every component in memo without measuring.
Passing inline objects or functions to memoised children, silently defeating memoisation.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A component re-renders when its own state changes, its parent re-renders, or a consumed context changes; re-rendering is not the same as DOM updating, since React diffs first. React.memo skips re-rendering when props are shallowly unchanged, useMemo caches expensive computed values, and useCallback caches function identity so memoised children do not see a new prop every render. These only help when the work is expensive or when they prevent a large subtree from re-rendering, and they add comparison cost otherwise. The correct workflow is to profile first, fix the measured bottleneck — which may be bundle size, a network waterfall, or a huge list needing virtualization — and re-measure.
followUps: Why does an inline arrow function prop defeat React.memo?
How would you reduce a large initial bundle?
interviewQuestions.question: How do React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback work, and when should you not use them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: They cache renders, values, and function identities respectively, but only pay off for expensive work or large subtrees — measure with the Profiler first.
tips: Explain the shallow, referential comparison — that is the key mechanic.
Name a non-render bottleneck (bundle size, lists) to show you optimise the right thing.
interviewQuestions.title: Memoization and React performance

commonMistakes: Using array indexes as keys for reorderable lists.
Assuming re-render means DOM update — React diffs first and usually changes little.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Rendering means calling a component to produce elements; committing means applying the diff to the DOM. React's reconciler matches the new tree against the previous one, using keys to identify list items across renders. Stable, unique keys let React reuse DOM nodes and preserved component state correctly when items are inserted, removed, or reordered; index keys tie identity to position, so reordering gives the wrong item the wrong state and focus. State itself is preserved by position in the tree, so moving a component to a different position resets its state even if its type is unchanged.
followUps: What happens to state when a component moves position in the tree?
How does React decide which DOM nodes to update?
interviewQuestions.question: How does React reconciliation work, and why do keys matter?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: React diffs the new element tree against the old one and patches only what changed; stable keys let it match list items correctly across renders.
tips: Use the reorderable list example to make the index-key failure concrete.
Distinguish rendering from committing.
interviewQuestions.title: Reconciliation and keys

commonMistakes: Claiming one machine can scale forever, or that adding machines is free.
Designing for unstated or infinite scale instead of the numbers given.
Forgetting the load balancer itself can be a single point of failure.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine: simple, no architecture change, but capped by the largest machine available and still a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds machines behind a load balancer: far more headroom, but it forces stateless servers, shared or partitioned state, health checking, and failure containment. In practice, scale vertically while it is cheap and sufficient, and horizontally once one machine becomes a bottleneck or a risk. Name the trigger explicitly: a measured limit, a failure concern, or a growth forecast, not a fashion preference.
followUps: What has to change in the application before horizontal scaling works?
How do you make the load balancer itself redundant?
interviewQuestions.question: When would you scale vertically versus horizontally, and what changes when you switch?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Scale up while one machine is cheap and sufficient; scale out with stateless servers behind a redundant load balancer once a single machine bottlenecks or risks the whole system.
tips: Name a concrete trigger for switching, such as a measured bottleneck or a single point of failure.
Mention statelessness as the enabler of horizontal scaling.
interviewQuestions.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling

commonMistakes: Treating CAP as a one-time global choice for the whole system.
Claiming a system can have all three properties during a partition.
Ignoring that most systems are consistent in normal operation and only face the trade-off during a partition.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: During a network partition, a distributed store can guarantee at most two of consistency (every read sees the latest write), availability (every request gets a non-error response), and partition tolerance (the system keeps working). Partitions happen in real networks, so the practical choice is consistency versus availability while partitioned, made per dataset: a bank balance should refuse a request rather than risk a wrong balance, while a social feed should answer with slightly stale data rather than fail. Many systems are eventually consistent, converging shortly after a write, which is fine where staleness is harmless and unacceptable where it is not.
followUps: Give one dataset where you would choose consistency and one where you would choose availability.
What does eventual consistency mean for a user who just posted?
interviewQuestions.question: Explain the CAP theorem and how you would apply it to a real system.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: During a partition, choose consistency or availability per dataset: refuse requests to stay correct, or serve possibly stale data to stay up.
tips: Apply it per dataset, not once for the whole system.
Give a concrete example for each side of the trade-off.
interviewQuestions.title: CAP theorem in practice

commonMistakes: Quoting a final number with no assumptions shown.
Estimating average load but forgetting a peak multiplier.
Designing for infinite scale instead of the stated numbers.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start from stated assumptions: daily active users, actions per user per day, and a peak multiplier (often 2-5x the average). For example, 10 million daily users making 20 requests each gives 200 million requests per day, about 2,300 per second on average, and about 7,000 per second at 3x peak. Multiply by response size for bandwidth and by retention for storage. Show the arithmetic so the interviewer can challenge an assumption rather than a mystery number, and say what would change the answer: more users, larger payloads, or a higher peak.
followUps: How would your estimate change if traffic were event-driven, like a live sports final?
Which of your assumptions is most uncertain, and how would you validate it?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you estimate capacity for a system you have never built?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: From daily users, actions per user, and a peak multiplier, derive requests per second, bandwidth, and storage, showing each assumption.
tips: Write the arithmetic out loud; the method matters more than the final number.
Use round numbers and a peak factor.
interviewQuestions.title: Back-of-envelope capacity estimation

commonMistakes: Caching everything, including data that changes constantly.
Treating the cache as the source of truth, so eviction becomes data loss.
Invalidating before writing to the database, letting a concurrent read re-cache the old value.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Cache-aside is the most common pattern: the application checks the cache, falls back to the database on a miss, populates the cache, and invalidates on write (database first, then invalidate, with a TTL as a safety net). Write-through writes cache and database together, so the cache is never stale but writes are slower. Write-behind writes to cache and flushes asynchronously, which is fast but risks loss if the cache crashes first. Choose from staleness tolerance: a feed can be minutes stale, a balance cannot. The classic failure is the thundering herd, when many requests miss on one hot key at once; mitigate with a lock or coalescing, jittered TTLs, or proactive warming.
followUps: How do you bound staleness if explicit invalidation misses a key?
What happens to your design if the cache cluster goes down?
interviewQuestions.question: Compare cache-aside, write-through, and write-behind, and how do you handle a thundering herd?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Cache-aside is the flexible default; write-through is never stale but slower; write-behind is fast but can lose data. Bound staleness with a TTL and break herds with coalescing or jitter.
tips: Order writes database-first, then invalidate.
Name the thundering herd without being asked; it shows production awareness.
interviewQuestions.title: Caching patterns and thundering herds

commonMistakes: Assuming a queue gives exactly-once delivery.
Building a consumer that double-charges on redelivery.
Retrying failures forever instead of parking them in a dead-letter queue.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A queue decouples producers from consumers: a request can return after enqueueing while workers process asynchronously, absorbing bursts and surviving consumer outages. Delivery guarantees matter: at-most-once can lose messages, at-least-once can deliver duplicates, and exactly-once is effectively at-least-once plus idempotent consumers with deduplication. So consumers must be idempotent, ideally with the deduplication check and the side effect in one transaction, and repeatedly failing messages should go to a dead-letter queue for inspection after a retry limit. Ordering is a separate choice: global ordering is expensive, and ordering per key or partition is usually enough.
followUps: How would you make an order-placement consumer safe against redelivery?
When would you need ordering, and at what granularity?
interviewQuestions.question: Why must queue consumers be idempotent, and what delivery guarantees do queues offer?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: At-least-once delivery redelivers after crashes, so consumers must be idempotent; exactly-once is at-least-once plus idempotency and deduplication.
tips: Give a concrete double-charge or double-booking example.
Mention dead-letter queues for poison messages.
interviewQuestions.title: Queue delivery guarantees and idempotency

commonMistakes: Choosing NoSQL because it sounds scalable, then reimplementing joins in application code.
Sharding before replicas and a cache have been shown insufficient.
Choosing a low-cardinality shard key that creates hot shards.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start from the access pattern. SQL fits data where relationships, constraints, and multi-row transactions matter: orders, payments, inventory. NoSQL fits flexible schemas and specialised patterns: documents for evolving hierarchical data, key-value for sessions and caches, wide-column for massive sparse tables, graph for heavily connected data. Scale in order: one relational database, then read replicas and a cache for reads, then sharding for writes, on a high-cardinality key aligned with the dominant query pattern. Most real systems use both: SQL for the transactional core, NoSQL alongside for catalogues, sessions, or feeds.
followUps: What happens to a read replica that lags behind the primary?
How do you handle a query that now spans many shards?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL, and when do you shard?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: SQL for relational, transactional data; NoSQL for flexible or specialised access. Replicate and cache first; shard for writes only when forced, on a well-distributed key.
tips: Justify from read/write ratios and consistency needs, not fashion.
Name the hot-shard risk of a bad shard key.
interviewQuestions.title: SQL vs NoSQL and when to shard

commonMistakes: Drawing the architecture before clarifying requirements.
Estimating nothing, then over- or under-building.
Putting analytics on the synchronous redirect path.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Clarify first: features, users, read/write ratio, latency and consistency needs, and what is out of scope. Estimate: 100 million URLs per month is about 40 creations per second on average, and redirects dominate, so this is read-heavy. For short codes, either hash the long URL (handling collisions) or encode a counter id in base62 (unique by construction, needing an available counter). Serve redirects from a cache in front of a replicated database, and move click analytics behind a queue so analytics can never slow or fail a redirect. End by naming the bottleneck: the counter service or primary on writes, and hot keys on the cache.
followUps: How do you support custom aliases without collisions?
What if a single short link goes viral?
interviewQuestions.question: Design a URL shortener.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Read-heavy system: base62 codes from a counter or a hash, cached redirects in front of replicated storage, and analytics moved behind a queue.
tips: State the read/write ratio before choosing components.
Keep analytics off the hot path.
interviewQuestions.title: Design a URL shortener

commonMistakes: Choosing push or pull absolutely, with no answer for celebrities.
Building a ranking pipeline nobody asked for when the requirement was chronological.
Ignoring that storage grows with followers times posts under push.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The central tension is fan-out. Push (fan-out on write) precomputes each follower's feed, so reads are a single lookup, but publishing costs one write per follower and storage grows with followers times posts. Pull (fan-out on read) makes writes cheap but reads must gather and merge posts from everyone followed. The standard answer is a hybrid: push for ordinary users, a pull path for celebrities whose follower counts make push infeasible, with hot feeds cached. Then clarify ranking: chronological is simple, while ranked feeds need scoring computed offline or near-real-time and merged at read time.
followUps: How do you handle a user who follows ten thousand accounts under pull?
Where does ranking happen if the feed is ranked rather than chronological?
interviewQuestions.question: Design a news feed. How do you handle a celebrity with millions of followers?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Push for fast reads, pull for cheap writes, and a hybrid for celebrities: push for ordinary users, a pull path for high-follower accounts.
tips: Name the cost of each approach in writes and reads before choosing.
Ask whether the feed is chronological or ranked.
interviewQuestions.title: Design a news feed

commonMistakes: Promising global ordering across all conversations, which nobody needs.
Treating presence as exact, when best-effort is fine.
Losing offline messages instead of storing and delivering on reconnect.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Use gateway servers holding persistent WebSocket connections, with messages stored durably and fanned out to recipients' connections. Ordering is per conversation, via a sequence number assigned by a single writer or a partitioned log; global ordering across conversations is not a sensible goal. Offline recipients receive stored messages on reconnect, so delivery does not depend on both parties being online. Presence is best-effort and eventually consistent: a user appearing online a second late is harmless, while a lost message is not. That distinction — what must be exact versus what may be approximate — is the judgement being tested.
followUps: How does a message reach a user connected to a different gateway server?
How do you handle a gateway server crashing with live connections?
interviewQuestions.question: Design a chat system with group messages and presence.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Gateway servers with persistent connections, durable per-conversation ordered storage for offline delivery, and best-effort presence.
tips: Distinguish exact requirements (message delivery, per-conversation order) from approximate ones (presence).
Mention the gateway routing problem explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: Design a chat system

commonMistakes: Creating a god class that parks cars, prices, and notifies.
Using inheritance where composition fits, then fighting the hierarchy.
Exposing public fields so invariants cannot be enforced.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start from the problem statement: nouns become candidate classes, verbs become methods, then filter out attributes masquerading as classes. Apply SOLID as a checklist: one reason to change per class, extension without modification, substitutable subclasses, small interfaces, dependencies on abstractions. For a parking lot: Vehicle, ParkingSpot, ParkingLot, Ticket, and a PricingStrategy interface, so a new pricing rule is a new class rather than an edit to parking logic. Enforce invariants inside objects (a spot cannot be both free and occupied) and synchronise the atomic claim of a spot so concurrent requests cannot double-book it.
followUps: Where would you put a new pricing rule, and what would you not change?
How do you handle two cars claiming the same spot at once?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you approach class design for a parking lot?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Nouns to classes, verbs to methods, then filter; one responsibility per class, pricing behind a Strategy interface, and an atomic, synchronised spot claim.
tips: Agree the class diagram before writing code.
Point to the interface that absorbs the next requirement.
interviewQuestions.title: Class design: parking lot

commonMistakes: Using inheritance for code reuse where composition would do.
Adding an interface with one implementation and no plausible second one.
Relying on callers to keep an object valid instead of enforcing invariants inside it.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Use inheritance only for a genuine is-a relationship where the subclass honours the parent contract (Liskov substitution); a subclass that throws for operations its parent promises breaks substitutability. Prefer composition for has-a relationships and for reuse, because it keeps classes loosely coupled and lets behaviour be swapped at runtime. Depend on interfaces where a second implementation is plausible — payment, pricing, notification — and skip the interface where there is exactly one and no test or extension need. Enforce invariants in constructors and methods so an object can never be in an invalid state, whatever its callers do.
followUps: Give an example where inheritance broke a design you have seen.
When is an interface overkill?
interviewQuestions.question: Inheritance versus composition: how do you decide?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Inheritance for true is-a with a honoured contract; composition for has-a and reuse, with interfaces at plausible variation points.
tips: Cite Liskov substitution, not just preference.
Admit when an interface is overkill.
interviewQuestions.title: Inheritance vs composition

commonMistakes: Applying a pattern to every class.
Using Singleton as a disguised global variable.
Confusing Adapter (interface conversion) with Decorator (layered behaviour).
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Strategy is the most useful LLD pattern: interchangeable algorithms (pricing, payment, notification) behind one interface, selected at runtime, so a new variant is a new class. Observer notifies many listeners without coupling the subject to them, but needs an unsubscribe path or it leaks. Decorator layers behaviour by wrapping while keeping the interface, unlike Adapter, which converts an incompatible interface into the one a client expects. Factory isolates creation logic that varies by type. Singleton should be rare: global mutable state hides dependencies and hardens testing, so prefer creating one instance and injecting it. A pattern must earn its place by solving a named problem; otherwise it is ceremony.
followUps: When would you choose Decorator over subclassing?
What goes wrong if observers are never unsubscribed?
interviewQuestions.question: Which design patterns do you reach for most in LLD, and when do you avoid them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Strategy for interchangeable algorithms, Observer for decoupled notification, Decorator for layered behaviour, Factory for varying creation; avoid patterns that solve no named problem, especially Singleton as global state.
tips: Name the problem before the pattern.
Show the cost of each pattern, not just its benefit.
interviewQuestions.title: Design patterns in LLD

commonMistakes: Implementing Observer without an unsubscribe path.
Writing a Factory that is just a switch with no abstraction benefit.
Saying Strategy while writing an if-else chain on a type field.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: In a Strategy, the client depends only on the interface and never inspects a type field; adding a variant adds a class and a registration, never an edit to existing logic. In Observer, the subject holds a list of observer interfaces and notifies them without knowing their concrete types, iterates over a copy to survive unsubscription during notification, and provides unsubscribe. In Decorator, each wrapper implements the same interface as the wrapped object and delegates to it, so decorators compose in any order. If your code has a switch on type at the decision point, you have described the pattern but not implemented it — the interviewer will notice.
followUps: How would you add a new payment method to a Strategy-based checkout?
How do you prevent an Observer notification from being blocked by one slow observer?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you know a Strategy or Observer implementation is genuinely following the pattern?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: No type switch at the decision point for Strategy, and for Observer a subject that notifies interfaces it does not know, with unsubscribe and safe iteration.
tips: Point to the exact code shape, not the pattern name.
Mention iterating over a copy during notification.
interviewQuestions.title: Implementing Strategy and Observer correctly

commonMistakes: Ignoring concurrency in booking and allocation problems.
Storing only balances instead of a transaction ledger.
Modelling state with scattered booleans instead of explicit states.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: For a parking lot, claim spots atomically per type, issue a ticket linking vehicle, spot, and entry time, and price behind a Strategy. For an elevator, keep a sorted request set and serve in the current direction first (SCAN), reversing only when that direction is exhausted. For ticket booking, the central difficulty is double booking: claim atomically, or hold the seat briefly and confirm or release on expiry. For expense sharing, record every expense as a ledger entry, derive balances from the ledger (never store only a balance), and settle greedily from the largest debtor to the largest creditor. For a library, index exactly the queries required and keep indexes updated on every write.
followUps: How do you prevent double booking of the last seat?
Why is a ledger better than storing only a balance?
interviewQuestions.question: Walk through your approach to parking lot, elevator, and Splitwise-style problems.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Same approach every time: clarify, entities, core flow, code, edge cases. Atomic claims for allocation, SCAN for elevators, ledgers and greedy settlement for expenses.
tips: Lead with the shared approach, then differentiate each problem.
Name the central difficulty of each problem explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: Common LLD problems

commonMistakes: Mixing raw values and matchers in one call, which throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException.
Mocking the class under test instead of its collaborators.
Verifying every internal call, making tests brittle.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A mock is a Mockito object with no real behaviour: you stub its answers with when(...).thenReturn(...) and optionally verify interactions with verify(...). A stub, in the strict vocabulary, returns canned answers without verification (in everyday Mockito usage, 'stubbing' just means programming a mock). A fake is a small real implementation, such as an in-memory repository backed by a HashMap, with genuine behaviour. A spy wraps a real object: real methods run unless you stub them. Choose a mock to verify a call or simulate a failure cheaply, a fake when simple stateful behaviour is worth reusing across tests, and a spy sparingly, when you cannot easily refactor to a seam.
followUps: When would you choose a fake over a mock?
Why is over-verifying interactions harmful?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a mock, a stub, a fake, and a spy?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A mock is a Mockito object with no real behaviour, used for stubbing and verification; a stub returns canned answers; a fake is a small real implementation; a spy wraps a real object and runs real methods unless stubbed.
tips: Give one concrete example of each, not just definitions.
Mention the fake example: an in-memory repository.
interviewQuestions.title: Mock vs stub vs fake vs spy

commonMistakes: Using when(...) on a void method, which cannot work because the call returns nothing.
Forgetting the doX().when(...) form for doNothing and doAnswer as well as doThrow.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: when(mock.voidMethod()) cannot work: Java evaluates the void call before Mockito sees it, and there is no return value for when to receive. The reverse form solves this: doThrow(new RuntimeException()).when(mock).voidMethod(args), and likewise doNothing().when(...) and doAnswer(...).when(...) for void methods. The same form is also needed when stubbing a method on a spy, because when(spy.method()) would execute the real method during stubbing.
followUps: Why is the doX().when(...) form also needed for spies?
How would you stub a void method to do nothing?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you stub a void method in Mockito to throw an exception, and why can you not use when() for it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use doThrow(...).when(mock).voidMethod(args), because when() cannot wrap a void call: the call returns nothing for when to receive.
tips: State the Java evaluation reason, not just the syntax.
Mention that the same form applies to spies.
interviewQuestions.title: Stubbing void methods in Mockito

commonMistakes: Saying matchers are a style preference rather than a mechanism with a stack.
Wrapping only some arguments in matchers and leaving others raw.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Mockito records argument matchers on an internal stack as they are evaluated during the stub or verify call. A raw value leaves no matcher on the stack, so Mockito cannot align the arguments with the matchers and throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException at runtime. The fix is to wrap every argument in a matcher: when(repo.find(anyString(), eq(10))). This applies equally to stubbing with when and to verification with verify.
followUps: What exception is thrown, and when: compile time or runtime?
How do you match an argument with a custom predicate?
interviewQuestions.question: Why can you not mix raw values and argument matchers in a single Mockito call?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Mockito records matchers on a stack as they are evaluated; a raw value leaves no matcher, so arguments cannot be aligned and Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException.
tips: Name the exception and that it is a runtime failure.
Show the fix: wrap every argument, e.g. eq(10).
interviewQuestions.title: Mockito matcher mixing rule

commonMistakes: Only testing happy paths and missing boundaries, nulls, and empty inputs.
Testing every private helper, coupling the suite to implementation details.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Good tests are FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, and Timely, plus readable and resilient to harmless refactoring. Design them around the public contract: group inputs into equivalence classes (sets expected to behave the same way), test one member of each, and add the boundary values between classes, where off-by-one errors cluster. For a percent valid in 0-100, that means -1 and 101 (invalid), 0 and 100 (boundaries), and a middle value. Name tests after behaviour and condition so failures are self-explanatory.
followUps: How do you choose inputs when you cannot test them all?
When is it acceptable to test a private method?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design a good unit test, and how do you choose which inputs to test?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Test the public contract with FIRST qualities: fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating, timely. Choose inputs by equivalence classes plus boundary values, where bugs cluster.
tips: Use the 0-100 percent example with -1, 0, 100, 101.
Mention that private-method testing is a sign the code should be extracted.
interviewQuestions.title: Test design and boundary values

commonMistakes: Saying the pyramid is about test count alone, ignoring cost and failure precision.
Recommending end-to-end tests for everything because they are most realistic.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Cost and speed increase up the pyramid while failure precision decreases: a unit test failure names the broken unit, while an end-to-end failure only says something in a whole flow broke. So most coverage belongs in cheap, precise unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle catch wiring and contract mistakes, and a few end-to-end tests at the top cover critical user journeys. A suite dominated by end-to-end tests is the ice-cream cone anti-pattern: slow, hard to debug, and eventually not run.
followUps: What is the ice-cream cone anti-pattern?
When is an end-to-end test worth its cost?
interviewQuestions.question: Why is the test pyramid shaped the way it is?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Cost and speed rise up the pyramid while failure precision falls, so most coverage belongs in cheap, precise unit tests, with fewer integration and end-to-end tests above them.
tips: Name the ice-cream cone anti-pattern unprompted.
Tie each layer to what it catches that the layer below cannot.
interviewQuestions.title: Test pyramid rationale

commonMistakes: Saying 'just re-run it' instead of diagnosing the cause.
Deleting a flaky test and silently losing its coverage.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A flaky test passes and fails without code changes, usually from shared mutable state, time dependence, un-awaited async work, randomness, or ordering assumptions. Each has a concrete cure: reset state in @BeforeEach and never rely on test order; inject a Clock and use Clock.fixed for time; await async conditions with a timeout instead of a guessed Thread.sleep; seed random generators and sort before asserting; mock or fake real network and file-system dependencies in unit tests. The process is quarantine the test so it does not block the suite, reproduce it, fix the root cause, and only then un-quarantine it.
followUps: What is the injected-Clock example for time-dependent flakiness?
When is quarantining better than deleting a flaky test?
interviewQuestions.question: What causes a flaky test, and how do you fix one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Shared state, time dependence, un-awaited async work, randomness, and ordering assumptions. Fix the root cause (injected Clock, awaited conditions, reset state), quarantine until fixed, and never just re-run or delete.
tips: Name at least two causes with their specific cures.
Use the Clock.fixed example; interviewers ask for it.
interviewQuestions.title: Flaky tests: causes and cures

commonMistakes: Reciting TDD as a universal rule without its costs.
Confusing TDD with simply writing tests after the code.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: TDD is the Red-Green-Refactor rhythm: write a failing test for the next behaviour, write the smallest code that passes, then refactor with the test as a safety net. Its real benefit is design pressure: code written to be testable tends to have small classes, explicit dependencies, and clear boundaries. Its costs are discipline and a slower first pass, and it fits poorly for exploratory work where the behaviour is not yet understood, since the test cannot be written before the behaviour is known. A balanced answer names both sides.
followUps: What design pressure does TDD create?
When would you not use TDD?
interviewQuestions.question: What is TDD, and when is it a good or poor fit?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: TDD is Red-Green-Refactor: failing test, minimal passing code, refactor. It drives testable design, but costs discipline and fits poorly when behaviour is still being discovered.
tips: Be honest about both benefit and cost.
Mention design pressure: small classes, explicit dependencies.
interviewQuestions.title: Test-driven development trade-offs

commonMistakes: Using @MockBean in new Spring Boot 3.4+ code, where it is deprecated.
Using @MockitoBean in a plain unit test, where there is no context.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer: controllers, filters, converters, and MVC infrastructure. Services and repositories are not loaded, so you replace them with @MockitoBean and test through MockMvc without starting a server. @SpringBootTest loads the full application context and is for behaviour that is the wiring itself. @MockitoBean is the Spring Boot 3.4+ replacement for the deprecated @MockBean, from org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito; it only makes sense where a context exists, so plain unit tests use @Mock instead.
followUps: Why can overusing @MockitoBean slow a suite?
What does @DataJpaTest load instead?
interviewQuestions.question: What does @WebMvcTest load, how does it differ from @SpringBootTest, and where does @MockitoBean fit?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer, with services replaced by @MockitoBean and tested via MockMvc; @SpringBootTest loads the full context. @MockitoBean is the Spring Boot 3.4+ replacement for deprecated @MockBean.
tips: Name the 3.4+ change and the new import package.
Mention context caching as the cost of overusing @MockitoBean.
interviewQuestions.title: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest and @MockitoBean

commonMistakes: Assuming @DataJpaTest uses the production database by default.
Testing a repository with a mocked repository, which verifies nothing about the query.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer: entities, repositories, and an embedded database by default, with each test running in a transaction that is rolled back afterwards so tests do not pollute each other. That rollback is what makes repository tests independent without manual cleanup. It is the right layer for verifying that a derived query method actually works, because a unit test with a mocked repository could never catch a misspelled query name. If the test must run against a real database, add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) and supply the datasource, for example from Testcontainers.
followUps: How do you make a @DataJpaTest run against Testcontainers PostgreSQL?
Why is rollback a problem for testing commit side effects?
interviewQuestions.question: What does @DataJpaTest load, and why is it transactional with rollback?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer against an embedded database, in a transaction rolled back afterwards, so repository tests stay independent and verify real query behaviour.
tips: Contrast with a mocked repository, which cannot catch a bad query.
Mention Replace.NONE as the bridge to Testcontainers.
interviewQuestions.title: @DataJpaTest and transactional rollback

commonMistakes: Forgetting Replace.NONE, so the test silently runs on the embedded database.
Hardcoding the internal port 5432 instead of using the mapped port.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Testcontainers starts real services in Docker containers for tests and removes them afterwards. In Spring Boot 3.1+, @ServiceConnection on a @Container field wires the container's connection details into the application context automatically, replacing hand-written @DynamicPropertySource registration for standard cases. Two details are essential: Docker maps the container's internal port to a random host port, so you must use the mapped port (or let @ServiceConnection handle it), and @DataJpaTest substitutes an embedded database by default, so you must add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) or the container is never actually used.
followUps: What happens if Docker is not available where tests run?
Why pin image tags to a major version instead of latest?
interviewQuestions.question: How do Testcontainers and Spring Boot connect, and what are the two details that most often go wrong?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @ServiceConnection (Spring Boot 3.1+) wires a container's connection details into the context automatically. The common mistakes are hardcoding the internal port instead of the mapped port, and forgetting Replace.NONE so @DataJpaTest silently uses an embedded database.
tips: Name both failure modes explicitly.
Mention that @DynamicPropertySource is the older, still-valid alternative.
interviewQuestions.title: Testcontainers with Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Putting every test in a container and losing the pyramid's speed benefit.
Using a shared dev database for tests, which reintroduces interference.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An embedded database such as H2 has a different SQL dialect and feature set from production PostgreSQL, so it tolerates queries production would reject and hides real failures. Testcontainers runs the actual production database in a disposable container, giving real fidelity with test isolation: each test class gets a fresh database, so tests cannot pollute each other. The price is Docker availability, slower startup, and more moving parts, so container tests belong in the integration layer and should be few and focused on database-specific behaviour. A shared dev or staging database is the option to avoid: tests interfere with each other and with developers.
followUps: When is an embedded database good enough?
How do you handle container tests in CI?
interviewQuestions.question: Why use Testcontainers instead of an embedded database, and when should you not use it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Testcontainers runs the real production database in a disposable container, catching dialect and feature differences an embedded database hides. Its cost (Docker, startup time) means it belongs only in focused integration tests.
tips: Give the H2-versus-PostgreSQL dialect example.
Name the shared-database anti-pattern as what not to do.
interviewQuestions.title: When Testcontainers is worth its cost

commonMistakes: Answering only about context caching, or only about test choice, without connecting them.
Recommending @SpringBootTest for everything because it is most faithful.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Choosing the smallest context that can catch the bug keeps the suite fast: unit tests for logic, slices for one layer, full context only for wiring. Context caching makes this concrete: Spring reuses a context across tests with identical configuration, but replacing different beans with @MockitoBean changes the context definition and forces expensive rebuilds, so overusing it across many test classes slows the suite even when each individual test is a slice test. The design rule that follows is to push logic down to plain unit tests, use @MockitoBean only at the boundary of a slice test, and keep full-context tests few.
followUps: How does Spring decide whether a context can be reused?
What test-only configuration alternatives avoid @MockitoBean?
interviewQuestions.question: How do test-layer choice and Spring context caching interact to determine suite speed?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Spring caches contexts with identical configuration; differing @MockitoBean replacements force expensive rebuilds. So push logic to unit tests, use @MockitoBean only at slice boundaries, and keep full-context tests few.
tips: Connect the caching mechanism to the practical rule.
Mention @TestConfiguration as an alternative for test-only beans with real behaviour.
interviewQuestions.title: Context caching and suite speed

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: JDK contains JRE, JRE contains JVM. Source compiles to bytecode with javac; the JVM loads, verifies, and executes bytecode, with JIT compilation for hot code. Portability comes from bytecode plus a platform-specific JVM. Remember: JDK is for development (compiler, tools), JRE is for running (libraries + JVM), JVM is the runtime engine itself. Class loading, bytecode verification, and the runtime memory areas (heap, stack, metaspace) are the usual follow-up topics.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: JDK, JRE, JVM in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM; source → bytecode → JVM execution → JIT for hot code.
tips: If asked 'is Java fully platform independent?', answer: bytecode is portable, but the JVM itself is platform-specific.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: JVM basics

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Encapsulation: bundle data with the methods that use it and expose it only through controlled access (private fields, public methods). Abstraction: expose what an object does, not how (abstract classes and interfaces). Inheritance: a subclass reuses and extends a superclass — favour composition over inheritance when reuse is not truly an is-a relationship. Polymorphism: the same call behaves differently by runtime type — method overriding (runtime) versus overloading (compile time). In an interview, always give a concrete example: e.g. a Payment interface with CardPayment and UpiPayment implementations, chosen at runtime.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: OOP in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Encapsulation hides state, abstraction hides complexity, inheritance reuses behaviour, polymorphism lets one interface take many forms.
tips: Name all four pillars, then immediately give one real example — interviewers remember examples, not definitions alone.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: OOP principles

commonMistakes: Comparing strings with == instead of equals().
Concatenating inside a loop instead of using StringBuilder.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: String is immutable: every concatenation creates a new object, so building strings in a loop with + is slow — use StringBuilder (single-threaded) or StringBuffer (synchronized). Literals are interned in the string pool, so "abc" == "abc" can be true, but never rely on it: compare content with equals(), and use equalsIgnoreCase() or Objects.equals() when nulls are possible. String is final, so it cannot be subclassed, which also makes it safe as a HashMap key. Know the common traps: String.split takes a regex, substring and trim return new strings, and string comparison with == is the classic interview bug.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Strings in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: String is immutable and pooled; use StringBuilder for loops, equals() for content, == only for reference identity.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Strings

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: List allows duplicates and is ordered; Set forbids duplicates; Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys. ArrayList gives fast random access; LinkedList is better for frequent inserts/removes in the middle but slow for random access. HashMap gives fast key lookup but no ordering guarantee — use LinkedHashMap for insertion order, TreeMap for sorted keys. HashSet is backed by a HashMap; TreeSet keeps elements sorted. ConcurrentHashMap is the thread-safe map choice, with no null keys or values, unlike HashMap (one null key, many null values) and Hashtable (synchronized, no nulls). Always state time complexity: ArrayList get is O(1), HashMap get/put is O(1) on average.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Collections in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: List: ordered + duplicates. Set: unique. Map: key-value. ArrayList for access, HashMap for lookup, ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.
tips: When asked 'which collection?', answer with the access pattern first: ordered? unique? keyed? thread-safe? — then name the class.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Collections

commonMistakes: Empty catch blocks.
Catching Exception before its subclasses, which does not compile.
Using exceptions for normal control flow.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Throwable splits into Error (serious JVM problems, do not catch) and Exception. Checked exceptions (e.g. IOException) must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and subclasses, e.g. NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) need not be declared. Use try-with-resources for anything AutoCloseable so resources close even on failure. Catch the most specific exception first — a broad catch of Exception hides bugs. Never swallow an exception with an empty catch block: log it or rethrow it, possibly wrapped. In Spring apps, prefer translating checked exceptions into meaningful runtime exceptions at service boundaries and handling them centrally with @ControllerAdvice.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Exceptions in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Checked exceptions must be handled or declared; unchecked (RuntimeException) need not be. Catch specific exceptions, use try-with-resources, never swallow exceptions.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Exceptions

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Generics let you write one class or method that works for many types while the compiler checks types for you — List<String> cannot accidentally hold an Integer. Because of type erasure, generic type information is removed at compile time: you cannot do new T(), check instanceof List<String>, or overload foo(List<String>) and foo(List<Integer>) together. Wildcards: <? extends T> is a producer (you read from it, PECS), <? super T> is a consumer (you write into it). Bounded type parameters (<T extends Comparable<T>>) restrict what a type argument may be. Generics do not work with primitives — use wrapper classes and autoboxing, and be aware of the small boxing cost in hot loops.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Generics in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Generics give compile-time type safety; type erasure means generic types do not exist at runtime. PECS: producer extends, consumer super.
tips: PECS is the single most-asked generics point: say it, then give an example (copying from List<? extends Number> into List<? super Number>).
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Generics

commonMistakes: Reusing a stream after a terminal operation.
Using forEach to mutate shared state inside a parallel stream.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A stream pipeline has a source (collection, array, generator), zero or more intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct — lazy, return a stream), and exactly one terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count, anyMatch — triggers execution). Streams do not modify the source and are single-use: reuse throws IllegalStateException. Intermediate operations are lazy, so filter().map() does nothing until a terminal operation runs, which enables short-circuiting with findFirst() or limit(). A lambda is shorthand for an anonymous implementation of a functional interface (one abstract method), e.g. (a, b) -> a + b for a Comparator. Method references (String::toUpperCase, System.out::println) are lambdas in shorter form. Parallel streams split work across threads, but only help for large, CPU-bound, stateless pipelines — never use them with shared mutable state.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Streams in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Streams are lazy pipelines: source → intermediate operations → one terminal operation. Lambdas are concise implementations of functional interfaces.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Streams and lambdas

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Optional is a container that is either empty or holds one non-null value: use Optional.ofNullable(value), map/flatMap to transform, orElse/orElseGet for a fallback, and orElseThrow for a meaningful exception. Prefer orElseGet over orElse when the fallback is expensive, because orElse evaluates eagerly. Never call get() without checking, never use Optional as a method parameter or a field in an entity, and never return null where you promised an Optional. The built-in functional interfaces: Predicate<T> (test, returns boolean), Function<T,R> (apply), Consumer<T> (accept, no result), Supplier<T> (get, no input), plus BiFunction, BiPredicate, and primitive versions like IntPredicate and ToIntFunction that avoid boxing. Custom functional interfaces need exactly one abstract method and are usually marked @FunctionalInterface.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Optional and functional interfaces in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Optional models 'value may be absent' explicitly. Core functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, plus Bi- variants and primitive specializations.
tips: If asked why not just return null: Optional forces the caller to handle absence at compile time instead of discovering a NullPointerException at runtime.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Optional and functional interfaces

commonMistakes: Creating unbounded threads instead of using a pool.
Assuming volatile makes compound actions atomic.
Forgetting to shut down an ExecutorService.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Each thread has its own stack; all threads share the heap, which is why unsynchronized access to shared mutable state causes race conditions. synchronized and ReentrantLock provide mutual exclusion; volatile guarantees visibility of a variable's latest value but not atomicity (volatile++ is still a race). Prefer the java.util.concurrent toolkit: ExecutorService and thread pools instead of new Thread(), ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList instead of synchronized wrappers, CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier for coordination, and CompletableFuture for async pipelines. Know the deadlock ingredients (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) and how to avoid them: acquire locks in a fixed order, use timeouts (tryLock), and keep critical sections small. Always shut down an ExecutorService, or the JVM will not exit.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Concurrency in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Threads share heap memory; synchronize access to shared mutable state, prefer java.util.concurrent utilities over raw wait/notify, and use ExecutorService instead of creating threads by hand.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Concurrency basics

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Without synchronization, one thread's write to a shared variable may never become visible to another thread, and the JVM or CPU may reorder operations. The Java Memory Model fixes this with happens-before relationships: a write happens-before a later read if they are ordered by a rule such as: unlocking a monitor happens-before locking the same monitor; a write to a volatile variable happens-before a later read of that volatile; starting a thread happens-before its first action; and a thread's last action happens-before another thread's join() on it. Practical consequences: publish shared state safely (final fields, volatile, or proper synchronization), do not rely on Thread.sleep() for visibility, and remember that 64-bit long/double reads and writes are atomic only if the field is volatile. Double-checked locking is correct only with a volatile instance field.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Java Memory Model in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The JMM defines when one thread's writes become visible to another. Happens-before rules — volatile, synchronized, thread start/join, final fields — are what guarantee visibility and ordering.
tips: Frame every JMM answer around one phrase: 'happens-before guarantees visibility and ordering; without it, there is no guarantee at all.'
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Java Memory Model

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Objects start in Eden (young generation); survivors move to survivor spaces and, after enough collections, are promoted to the old generation. Minor GC cleans the young generation and is frequent but cheap; major/full GC cleans the old generation and is rarer but costlier. Modern collectors: G1 (the default since Java 9, region-based, balances latency and throughput), ZGC and Shenandoah (very low pause times, good for large heaps). Reachability, not reference counting, decides liveness — even cyclic references are collected if unreachable. Practical points: avoid finalize() (deprecated, unpredictable), do not call System.gc() in production code, watch for memory leaks via static collections or unclosed listeners/caches holding references, and choose a collector by measuring pause time and throughput, not by reputation.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Garbage collection in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The GC reclaims unreachable objects. Most objects die young, so the heap is generational: young generation collected often, old generation rarely. Tune the collector to the app's latency or throughput goal.
tips: If asked 'how would you investigate high GC pauses?', answer: GC logs, heap dump analysis, and checking for allocation hotspots — in that order.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Garbage collection

commonMistakes: Deserializing untrusted input.
Forgetting serialVersionUID and then breaking compatibility on a class change.
Serializing fields that should be transient (passwords, caches).
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Reflection (Class, Method, Field) lets code inspect types, create instances, and call methods whose names are only known at runtime — frameworks like Spring and Jackson rely on it. Costs: slower than direct calls, breaks encapsulation (setAccessible), and defeats compile-time checking, so prefer it in framework code, not business logic. Serialization (java.io.Serializable) writes an object's state to a stream and reads it back; transient fields are skipped, static fields are not serialized, and serialVersionUID controls version compatibility — change the class without updating it and deserialization fails. Security warning: never deserialize untrusted data with native Java serialization; prefer JSON (Jackson) for data exchange. For deep copies, serialization works but is slow — consider a copy constructor or a mapping library instead.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Reflection and serialization in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Reflection inspects and invokes classes at runtime; serialization converts an object graph to bytes and back. Both are powerful and both bypass normal compile-time safety — use them deliberately.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Reflection and serialization

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The flow is: DriverManager (or a DataSource) gives a Connection, you create a Statement or PreparedStatement, execute a query, and read the ResultSet. Always prefer PreparedStatement over Statement: parameters are bound safely, which prevents SQL injection and lets the database reuse execution plans. Close Connection, Statement, and ResultSet in reverse order — try-with-resources does this for you. Handle SQLException (checked) by translating it into a meaningful application exception and rolling back the transaction where needed. In real applications, never open a raw connection per request: use a connection pool such as HikariCP (Spring Boot's default) and let Spring's JdbcTemplate or Spring Data JPA handle the boilerplate. Know the transaction basics: auto-commit off, commit on success, rollback on failure.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: JDBC in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: JDBC is Java's API for relational databases: load a driver, get a Connection, use PreparedStatement for parameterized SQL, close everything with try-with-resources, and pool connections in production.
tips: The one JDBC answer interviewers always want: PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection; Statement with string concatenation does not.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: JDBC

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: SOLID: S — a class has one reason to change; O — open for extension, closed for modification (extend via new code, not edits); L — a subclass must be usable wherever its superclass is expected; I — many small interfaces beat one fat interface; D — depend on abstractions, not concretions (this is what Spring DI implements). Patterns to name with an example each: Singleton (one instance — use an enum or Spring's singleton scope, not a hand-rolled double-checked lock unless asked); Factory (create objects without exposing construction logic); Builder (readable construction of objects with many optional fields); Strategy (swap algorithms at runtime, e.g. payment methods); Observer (notify subscribers of state changes); Decorator (add behaviour without subclassing); Adapter (make incompatible interfaces work together); Repository (abstract data access behind an interface). Never recite patterns without an example — one real use case each is what scores.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Design patterns and SOLID in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: SOLID: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion. Patterns to know cold: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Adapter, Repository.
tips: When asked for a pattern, name it, state the problem it solves, then give a one-line example from a real codebase.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Design patterns and SOLID

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Inversion of Control flips responsibility: instead of a class creating its own dependencies with new, the Spring container instantiates beans and injects their dependencies. Dependency injection comes in three forms — constructor injection (preferred: dependencies are final, the object is never half-built, and testing is easy), setter injection, and field injection (avoid: hidden dependencies, hard to test). Stereotype annotations mark beans for component scanning: @Component (general), @Service (business logic), @Repository (data access, also translates persistence exceptions), @Controller/@RestController (web layer). @Bean methods in a @Configuration class define beans explicitly, e.g. third-party classes you cannot annotate. Bean scopes: singleton (default, one per container), prototype (new instance per request), plus request/session scopes in web apps. Lifecycle hooks: @PostConstruct for setup after injection, @PreDestroy for cleanup.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Spring IoC in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: IoC means the container creates and wires beans instead of your code doing it. Inject via constructor (preferred), declare beans with @Component/@Service/@Repository or @Bean, and let Spring manage their lifecycle.
tips: If asked 'why constructor injection?', the answer is three words: immutability, testability, fail-fast — missing dependencies fail at startup, not at runtime.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring IoC and dependency injection

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: @SpringBootApplication is three annotations in one: @Configuration (this class defines beans), @EnableAutoConfiguration (let Boot configure beans for you), and @ComponentScan (find your @Component classes). Auto-configuration classes, listed in Spring Boot's auto-configuration imports, create beans only when conditions hold — @ConditionalOnClass (a library is present), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (you have not defined your own), @ConditionalOnProperty (a property is set). That is why adding spring-boot-starter-web gives you an embedded Tomcat and a DispatcherServlet with no XML, and why defining your own DataSource bean replaces Boot's default. Configuration comes from application.properties or application.yml, bound to type-safe classes with @ConfigurationProperties, and overridden per environment with Spring profiles (@Profile, spring.profiles.active). Debug with --debug or the conditions report to see which auto-configurations matched and why others did not.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Spring Boot auto-configuration in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @SpringBootApplication bundles @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. Auto-configuration supplies beans conditionally, based on what is on the classpath and what you have already defined.
tips: The killer interview line: auto-configuration backs off when you define your own bean — @ConditionalOnMissingBean is the mechanism.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring Boot auto-configuration

commonMistakes: Putting business logic in controllers.
Returning 200 for everything, including errors.
Using GET with a body or POST for pure reads.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The DispatcherServlet is the front controller: it receives every request, consults handler mappings to find the matching @Controller method, resolves arguments (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody), and writes the response via message converters (JSON with Jackson by default). @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody — it returns data, not views. REST conventions: GET for reads (200), POST for creation (201 with a Location header), PUT for full replacement, PATCH for partial updates, DELETE for removal (204), and 404 for missing resources, 400 for invalid input, 401/403 for auth problems. Validate request bodies with Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotNull, @Size) and return field errors cleanly. Centralize error handling with @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler so controllers stay focused on happy paths. Keep controllers thin: they translate HTTP to service calls and back, and all business logic lives in services.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Spring MVC and REST in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: DispatcherServlet routes requests to @RestController methods. Use @GetMapping/@PostMapping with proper status codes, validate input, and handle errors centrally with @ControllerAdvice.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring MVC and REST
