interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Define an interface extending JpaRepository<Entity, Id> and Spring Data generates the implementation at runtime: save, findById, findAll, delete, plus derived queries parsed from method names (findByEmailAndActiveTrue). For anything the naming rules cannot express, write @Query with JPQL or a native query. Entities map tables with @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue, and relationships @OneToMany/@ManyToOne — fetch type matters: LAZY loads associations on access, EAGER loads them immediately, and lazy access outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException. The N+1 problem (one query for parents, then one per child) is fixed with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection. Transactions belong on service methods with @Transactional (rollback by default only for unchecked exceptions), and read-only transactions (readOnly = true) are a cheap optimization for queries.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations from interfaces: derived query methods, @Query for custom JPQL, and @Transactional boundaries on services — with lazy loading and the N+1 problem as the classic traps.
tips: When asked about N+1, name the symptom (many small queries), the cause (lazy loading in a loop), and the fix (JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph) — all three in one breath.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute

commonMistakes: Storing secrets or passwords in a JWT payload.
Accepting tokens without verifying signature or expiry.
Storing passwords in plain text or with a fast hash like MD5.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Authentication (who are you?) happens first, via login credentials, OAuth2, or a token; authorization (what may you do?) follows, via roles or authorities (ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN). In Spring Security, a filter chain intercepts requests, an AuthenticationManager verifies credentials, and a SecurityContext holds the authenticated principal for the request. A JWT has three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as sub, roles, exp), and signature (HMAC or RSA over header + payload). The server verifies the signature with its secret or public key and rejects expired tokens — the payload is readable by anyone, so never put secrets in it. Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens (stored securely, ideally httpOnly) issue new ones. Stateless JWT auth scales because no server-side session is needed, but tokens cannot be revoked before expiry without a denylist — keep lifetimes short. Always serve auth over HTTPS, store passwords hashed with BCrypt (never plain or MD5), and protect against CSRF where cookies carry auth.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Security and JWT in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. JWT is a signed, stateless token: header.payload.signature — verify the signature and expiry, never trust the payload alone.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Security and JWT

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A microservice owns one bounded context and its own database — no shared tables across services, or you have a distributed monolith, not microservices. Services communicate synchronously (REST, gRPC) or asynchronously (events via Kafka/RabbitMQ); async messaging decouples services but introduces eventual consistency, so design for it (idempotent consumers, outbox pattern for reliable publishing). Cross-cutting concerns: an API gateway for routing and auth, service discovery for locating instances, centralized configuration, distributed tracing (trace IDs across calls), and resilience patterns — timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers. Spring Boot Actuator adds production endpoints: /actuator/health (liveness and readiness), /actuator/metrics (JVM, HTTP, custom counters via Micrometer), /actuator/info, and /actuator/env. Expose health publicly if needed, but restrict metrics and env behind authentication — they leak internals. Pair Actuator with Prometheus/Grafana for metrics and a log aggregator for logs.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Microservices and Actuator in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services, each owning its data. Actuator exposes health, metrics, and info endpoints so you can observe them — but expose only what is safe.
tips: If asked 'monolith or microservices?', answer with trade-offs: microservices buy independent scaling and deployment but cost operational complexity — do not present them as always better.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Microservices and Actuator

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Records (Java 16) are concise immutable data carriers: record Point(int x, int y) {} generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString — use them for DTOs and value objects, not for mutable entities. Sealed classes (Java 17) restrict which classes may extend them (permits), making hierarchies exhaustive for switch expressions. Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16) removes casts: if (obj instanceof String s) { use s directly }. Switch expressions (Java 14) return values and support arrow syntax, and pattern matching for switch (Java 21) matches on types and guards. Text blocks (Java 15) write multiline strings with """ without escaping every quote — ideal for SQL and JSON samples. var (Java 10) infers local variable types but is not dynamic typing and cannot be used for fields or method signatures. Virtual threads (Java 21) make blocking-style code scale to millions of threads, but do not fix shared-state bugs — synchronization rules still apply.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Modern Java features in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Records for data carriers, sealed classes for closed hierarchies, pattern matching for instanceof and switch, text blocks for multiline strings, and var for local type inference.
tips: Name the Java version for each feature — interviewers use version numbers to check whether knowledge is current.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Modern Java features

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: JDK is for development and includes the compiler and tools plus the JRE. JRE is for running Java and includes the JVM plus libraries. JVM is the engine that loads and executes bytecode, managing memory and garbage collection. Bytecode is platform-independent; the JVM is platform-specific, which is why the same bytecode runs on different operating systems with a JVM for each.
followUps: Is Java compiled or interpreted?
What does the bytecode verifier do?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: JDK is for developing (compiler + JRE), JRE is for running (JVM + libraries), and JVM is the engine that executes bytecode.
tips: Draw the nesting: JDK contains JRE, JRE contains JVM.
Mention bytecode portability explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: JDK, JRE, JVM

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: String is immutable: operations like toUpperCase or concat return a new String instead of changing the original. This makes strings safe to share, safe as map keys (hashCode can be cached), and thread-safe. String literals are interned in the string pool, so two equal literals may share one object — but you should still compare contents with equals, not ==, which compares references.
followUps: When would you use StringBuilder instead?
Why is immutability important for HashMap keys?
interviewQuestions.question: Why is String immutable in Java?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: For security, thread safety, hashCode caching, and safe sharing — operations on a String return a new String instead of modifying it.
tips: Give a concrete example: a string used as a map key must not change after insertion.
interviewQuestions.title: String immutability

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A HashMap stores entries in buckets chosen by the key's hash. In Java 8+, a bucket starts as a linked list and converts to a balanced tree when collisions grow (8 entries with at least 64 buckets), keeping worst-case lookup from degrading linearly. Equal keys must have equal hash codes, and a key's hash code must not change while it is in the map — hence immutable keys are preferred. HashMap allows one null key; ConcurrentHashMap allows neither null keys nor null values.
followUps: What happens when two keys collide?
Why must equals and hashCode be consistent?
interviewQuestions.question: How does HashMap work internally?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Entries go into buckets by hash; buckets treeify under collision pressure in Java 8+, and keys must keep equals/hashCode consistent.
tips: Mention treeification threshold and the immutable-key rule — interviewers listen for both.
interviewQuestions.title: HashMap internals

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct) are lazy and return a new stream; they do nothing until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, findFirst) runs. A stream is consumed by its terminal operation and cannot be reused — reusing it throws IllegalStateException. Short-circuiting terminals like findFirst or anyMatch can stop processing early.
followUps: When would you avoid parallel streams?
What is the difference between map and flatMap?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal stream operations?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Intermediate operations are lazy and return a stream; terminal operations trigger execution and consume the stream.
tips: Name one example of each, and mention that reuse throws IllegalStateException.
interviewQuestions.title: Stream operations

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Inversion of Control means the Spring container creates objects (beans) and supplies their dependencies, instead of each class creating its own with new. Dependency Injection is how it does that, preferably through constructors. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, required, and final, and makes testing easy because you can pass a mock directly. Field injection hides dependencies and is discouraged in new code.
followUps: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
What happens when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton?
interviewQuestions.question: What is Inversion of Control, and why is constructor injection preferred?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: IoC means the container creates and wires beans; constructor injection is preferred because dependencies are explicit, required, final, and easy to test.
tips: Contrast with field injection explicitly — interviewers expect that comparison.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring IoC and DI

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Auto-configuration classes are guarded by conditions — for example @ConditionalOnClass (a class is on the classpath), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (no user bean of that type exists), and @ConditionalOnProperty. If you define your own bean of the same type, auto-configuration backs off for that bean. That is how Spring Boot provides sensible defaults that you can override. The --debug report shows which auto-configurations applied and why others did not.
followUps: What is a starter?
How do you debug a missing auto-configured bean?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work, and how do you override it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Auto-configuration applies conditionally (classpath, missing bean, property); defining your own bean of the same type makes it back off.
tips: Mention @ConditionalOnMissingBean by name — it is the mechanism behind 'your bean wins'.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Boot auto-configuration

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Loading N parent entities and then lazily loading a collection for each one produces 1 + N queries — the N+1 problem. Fix it with a fetch join (JOIN FETCH), an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection that fetches exactly what is needed. Do not fix it by making everything EAGER, which loads data you may never use. Also, accessing a lazy collection after the transaction closes throws LazyInitializationException.
followUps: What is the difference between lazy and eager loading?
Why does @Transactional not work on a private method?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the N+1 problem in JPA, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: 1 query for parents plus N queries for children; fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection — not blanket EAGER.
tips: Name the fix and the anti-pattern (blanket EAGER) in the same answer.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA N+1 problem

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and visibility: only one thread holds a given monitor at a time, and writes before releasing the lock are visible to the next thread acquiring it. volatile provides visibility only: writes are visible to other threads, but compound actions like count++ (read-modify-write) are still not atomic. For atomic single-variable updates, use AtomicInteger and friends, or a lock.
followUps: Why is a plain counter unsafe across threads?
What is a happens-before relationship?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between synchronized and volatile?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: synchronized gives exclusion plus visibility; volatile gives visibility only, not atomicity for compound actions.
tips: Use count++ as the concrete counterexample for volatile.
interviewQuestions.title: synchronized vs volatile

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Checked exceptions must be declared or handled, and they are meant for recoverable conditions such as a missing file or a failed network call, while unchecked exceptions usually signal programming errors such as a null dereference or an illegal argument. Overusing checked exceptions leaks implementation details through every caller, so many modern codebases wrap them in a meaningful unchecked exception at a boundary. Try-with-resources guarantees that each resource is closed in reverse order of opening, even when an exception occurs, and any exception thrown during close is added as a suppressed exception rather than hiding the original failure. Always close resources you open, log the original exception with context, and avoid catching Exception just to swallow it.
followUps: When would you wrap a checked exception instead of declaring it?
How do you inspect a suppressed exception?
interviewQuestions.question: When should you use a checked exception versus an unchecked exception, and how does try-with-resources change exception handling?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Checked for recoverable conditions, unchecked for programming errors; try-with-resources closes resources reliably and preserves the original exception, adding close failures as suppressed exceptions.
tips: Name a concrete recoverable case and a concrete programming-error case.
Mention suppressed exceptions — it shows you have debugged real resource code.
interviewQuestions.title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: HashMap is not thread-safe and its iterators are fail-fast, so a concurrent modification during iteration usually throws ConcurrentModificationException, whereas ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent and tolerate concurrent updates without throwing. ConcurrentHashMap also forbids null keys and null values, because a null return from get would be ambiguous when another thread could have removed the entry. Its atomic methods such as computeIfAbsent, merge, and putIfAbsent let you update a shared map without external locking, but the mapping function must be short and side-effect free, since it may be retried. For counters or grouped results, combine it with atomic values such as LongAdder or a concurrent collection rather than synchronizing the whole map.
followUps: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and values?
When is computeIfAbsent unsafe?
interviewQuestions.question: How does ConcurrentHashMap differ from a synchronized HashMap, and when would you choose it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: ConcurrentHashMap is lock-striped, thread-safe, weakly consistent for iteration, and forbids nulls; a synchronized HashMap serializes all access and still fails fast on concurrent iteration.
tips: Contrast fail-fast with weakly consistent iteration explicitly.
Warn that computeIfAbsent functions must be short and side-effect free.
interviewQuestions.title: ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronized HashMap

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Parallel streams split work across the common ForkJoinPool, which helps only for large, CPU-bound, splittable workloads with independent, non-blocking operations. They hurt when the source is small, the work is I/O-bound, the operations block, or the pipeline uses stateful operations such as sorted or distinct that force coordination, and they can starve other tasks sharing the common pool. Stateful lambda side effects, such as appending to a shared list, break correctness in parallel pipelines, so collect results with a proper collector instead. A good answer names the workload, checks its size, avoids blocking calls, and measures before and after rather than assuming parallelism is faster.
followUps: Why should you not do blocking I/O inside a parallel stream?
How do you collect results safely from a parallel stream?
interviewQuestions.question: When does a parallel stream help, and when does it make performance worse?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Parallel streams help only for large CPU-bound work over a splittable source; they hurt for small, blocking, or I/O-bound work and can starve the shared common pool.
tips: Give the three conditions: large, CPU-bound, splittable.
Mention that the common ForkJoinPool is shared, so a slow stream affects the whole application.
interviewQuestions.title: Parallel streams: help or harm

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: CompletableFuture chains such as thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine let you express dependent and independent async steps without blocking, while exceptionally and handle let you recover or translate failures at a defined point in the chain. The most common production failure is submitting many futures to an unbounded or too-small pool, so dependent stages queue up and the whole pipeline stalls even though no thread has deadlocked. Always supply an explicit executor for blocking or long-running stages, bound the pool and its queue, set timeouts with orTimeout, and decide where exceptions are observed, because an unobserved future failure is silently lost. For fan-out work, combine futures with allOf and then inspect each result individually rather than assuming success.
followUps: What happens when a CompletableFuture exception is never observed?
Why should blocking stages not use the common ForkJoinPool?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you chain CompletableFuture stages safely in production, and what usually goes wrong?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Chain with thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine, handle failures explicitly, use a dedicated bounded executor for blocking stages, and apply timeouts.
tips: Name the thread-pool exhaustion failure mode, not just the API methods.
Mention orTimeout and explicit exception handling in the same answer.
interviewQuestions.title: CompletableFuture in production

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Most modern collectors divide the heap into young and old generations, because most objects die young: short-lived objects are collected cheaply in the young generation, while survivors are promoted to the old generation, which is collected less often but more expensively. G1 divides the heap into regions and targets a pause-time goal by collecting the regions with the most garbage first, whereas the Parallel collector prioritizes throughput and accepts longer pauses. Frequent full garbage collections, long promotion failures, or a steadily growing old generation usually point to a leak, an undersized heap, or objects that live longer than expected. Tune by measuring pause times and allocation rates first, then adjust heap size and collector choice, rather than guessing flags.
followUps: How do you tell a leak apart from a heap that is simply too small?
When would you prefer throughput over low pause time?
interviewQuestions.question: How do generational garbage collectors work, and how do you choose between G1 and Parallel GC?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Young objects are collected cheaply and survivors are promoted; G1 targets pause time with region-based collection, Parallel targets throughput with longer pauses.
tips: Explain the generational hypothesis before naming collectors.
Tie the choice to a measurable goal: pause time versus throughput.
interviewQuestions.title: Generational GC and collector choice

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Singleton is the default scope, so the container creates one instance per application context, while prototype creates a new instance on every request for the bean. The classic trap is injecting a prototype bean into a singleton: the injection happens once, so the singleton keeps the same prototype instance forever. Fix it by injecting a provider, such as ObjectProvider or Provider, and asking for a fresh instance on each use, or by using a scoped proxy. Request and session scopes only exist in a web context, and relying on them in a service layer makes the service untestable outside a request, so keep scope decisions at the edge where they belong.
followUps: How do you get a fresh prototype instance inside a singleton?
Why is request scope a poor fit for a service bean?
interviewQuestions.question: What goes wrong when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The singleton captures one prototype instance at injection time; inject ObjectProvider or Provider and request a fresh instance per use, or use a scoped proxy.
tips: State the trap first, then the fix — interviewers want both.
Mention that prototype beans are not destroyed by the container.
interviewQuestions.title: Prototype beans in singletons

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring Boot resolves configuration from many sources in a defined precedence order, roughly: command-line arguments and environment variables beat application properties files, which beat packaged defaults, and profile-specific files such as application-prod.properties beat the base application.properties within the same source type. Binding properties into a validated @ConfigurationProperties class is safer than scattering @Value annotations, because it groups related settings, supports relaxed binding and type conversion, and fails fast on invalid values when validation is enabled. Secrets should come from environment variables or a secret store, never from a committed properties file, and profile-specific behaviour should be expressed as configuration, not as if-statements scattered through code. When a value surprises you, check the active profiles and the effective property source order before assuming the code is wrong.
followUps: Where should secrets live, and why not in application.properties?
How do you fail fast on invalid configuration?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring Boot decide which configuration value wins, and how should you structure configuration for multiple environments?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Higher-precedence sources such as command-line arguments and environment variables beat properties files, and profile-specific files beat the base file; bind settings into validated @ConfigurationProperties classes.
tips: Recite the precedence order in one sentence.
Recommend @ConfigurationProperties over scattered @Value.
interviewQuestions.title: Profiles and configuration precedence

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A @RestControllerAdvice class centralizes exception handling across controllers, mapping each exception type to a consistent error body and HTTP status, so controllers stay focused on happy-path logic. Bean Validation annotations such as @NotNull, @Size, and @Pattern on a request DTO, triggered by @Valid, reject bad input before business logic runs, and validation failures arrive as a MethodArgumentNotValidException you can translate in the same advice class. Return ResponseEntity when the status or headers vary, such as 201 Created with a Location header after creating a resource, and keep error bodies stable with fields for a code, a message, and request context. Never leak stack traces or internal exception messages to clients, and never use exceptions for ordinary control flow.
followUps: Where does validation run relative to controller logic?
What should a stable API error body contain?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design consistent error handling and validation for a Spring MVC REST API?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Validate DTOs with Bean Validation, translate exceptions centrally in @RestControllerAdvice into stable error bodies, and use ResponseEntity when status or headers vary.
tips: Pair validation and exception translation — they belong together in the answer.
Mention 201 with a Location header as the ResponseEntity example.
interviewQuestions.title: REST error handling and validation

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Derived query methods are readable for simple lookups, but they grow unwieldy for complex conditions, so use @Query for explicit JPQL or native SQL, and projections or DTO queries when you only need a few columns. Pagination with Pageable is convenient, but offset pagination degrades on large tables because the database still scans skipped rows, so keyset pagination on an ordered unique key is better for infinite-scroll or export workloads. Keep transaction boundaries at the service layer, not the repository, so a unit of work that touches several repositories commits or rolls back together, and avoid lazy-loading collections inside a controller after the transaction has closed. Count queries for Page results can also be expensive, so use Slice or a separate count only when the total is actually displayed.
followUps: When is keyset pagination better than offset pagination?
Why should transactions live at the service layer?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose between derived queries, @Query, and pagination strategies in Spring Data JPA?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Derived queries for simple lookups, @Query for complex or selective queries, offset pagination for small result sets, and keyset pagination for large or scrolling workloads.
tips: Name the offset-pagination cost: skipped rows are still scanned.
Put transactions at the service layer, not the repository.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA queries and pagination

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A microservice deployment typically needs service discovery so instances can find each other as they scale, centralized configuration so behaviour changes without redeploying, and a resilience layer with timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers. Timeouts bound how long you wait, retries help only for transient and idempotent failures, and a circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency so it can recover instead of being overwhelmed by retries. Retrying a non-idempotent operation, such as a payment, without an idempotency key can duplicate its effect, so retry policy and idempotency must be designed together. Health endpoints and distributed tracing are what let you find the failing service in the first place, so treat observability as part of the design, not an afterthought.
followUps: When is a retry dangerous rather than helpful?
How do a timeout, a retry, and a circuit breaker complement each other?
interviewQuestions.question: What resilience patterns does a microservice need, and when does each one apply?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Service discovery, centralized configuration, timeouts to bound waits, retries only for transient idempotent failures, and circuit breakers to stop overwhelming a failing dependency.
tips: Distinguish retries from circuit breakers by their purpose.
Flag non-idempotent retries, such as payments, as the classic mistake.
interviewQuestions.title: Microservice resilience patterns

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An inner join returns only rows with a match on both sides, a left join keeps every row from the left table and fills unmatched right-side columns with null, and a full outer join keeps unmatched rows from both sides. To find duplicates, group by the candidate columns and keep only groups whose count is greater than one; to find orphan rows, use a left join and filter for null on the right side, or an anti-join with NOT EXISTS. Indexes speed up filtered and joined columns, but every index slows writes and costs storage, so index the columns your queries actually filter and join on, and verify with an execution plan rather than guessing. A common mistake is joining on a column with a different type or collation, which silently prevents index use.
followUps: How would you find customers with no orders?
Why can adding an index make some queries slower?
interviewQuestions.question: How do join types differ, and how would you find duplicate and orphan rows in SQL?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Inner keeps only matches, left keeps all left rows with nulls for misses, full outer keeps both sides; find duplicates with GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT greater than one, orphans with a left join filtered to null.
tips: Give the orphan-row query pattern, not just the join definitions.
Mention checking the execution plan before adding indexes.
interviewQuestions.title: SQL joins, duplicates, and orphans

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The task is to group words that are anagrams of each other, for example listen and silent. The idiomatic approach is a single pass over the input: for each word, build a canonical key by sorting its characters or by counting character frequencies, then append the word to the list stored under that key in a hash map. Sorting gives a key in time proportional to word length times log word length, while a frequency count gives a linear-time key and is preferable for long words. At the end, return the map values as the groups. A common mistake is comparing words pairwise, which is quadratic, or using the unsorted word itself as the key, which never groups anything.
followUps: How would you improve the key for very long words?
How does the complexity change if the alphabet is tiny, such as lowercase letters only?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: group a list of words into sets of anagrams. What is your approach and its complexity?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Build a canonical key per word, by sorted characters or character counts, and collect words into a hash map keyed by that key; each word is processed once.
tips: State the key idea first — the rest of the solution follows from it.
Compare sorting versus counting keys to show you considered trade-offs.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: group anagrams

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start by reproducing the slowness with a realistic request and measuring where time goes: check application metrics for thread-pool saturation, database connection-pool waits, and cache hit rates, and enable slow-query logging before changing anything. The usual culprits, in order, are an N+1 query pattern introduced by a new feature, a missing index on a newly filtered column, an unbounded result set being serialized, and a downstream call without a timeout. Fix the query or add the index, page or limit the result, add a timeout and a cache only where the data tolerates staleness, and verify with the same measurement you started from. A common mistake is adding caching or scaling instances first, which hides the bad query and spreads its cost across more machines.
followUps: How do you confirm an N+1 problem rather than guessing?
When is adding a cache the wrong fix?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: a REST endpoint that used to respond in 200ms now takes 5 seconds under load, with no recent deployment. How do you investigate and fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Measure first — thread pool, connection pool, slow queries, cache hit rate — then fix the usual causes in order: N+1 queries, missing index, unbounded results, or a timeout-less downstream call.
tips: Lead with measurement, not with a fix.
Name the trap: scaling out before finding the bad query.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: suddenly slow API

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The Java Memory Model defines happens-before relationships that guarantee when one thread's writes become visible to another: unlocking a monitor happens before a later lock of the same monitor, writing a volatile variable happens before a later read of it, and starting a thread happens before anything in that thread. Double-checked locking was broken before Java 5 because the instance reference could become visible before the constructor finished, letting another thread observe a partially constructed object. Declaring the field volatile fixes it, because the volatile write of the reference happens after construction and is visible only after the object is fully initialized. In practice, prefer an enum singleton, a static holder class, or dependency injection over hand-rolled double-checked locking, and never rely on timing or sleep to order visibility.
followUps: Why was double-checked locking broken before Java 5?
What is a safe alternative to double-checked locking?
interviewQuestions.question: Why did double-checked locking need volatile, and what does happens-before guarantee?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Happens-before guarantees visibility between ordered actions; without volatile, another thread could see a partially constructed singleton, so volatile orders the reference publication after construction.
tips: Explain the partially constructed object problem concretely.
Recommend the enum singleton or static holder as the practical alternative.
interviewQuestions.title: Java Memory Model and double-checked locking

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: PECS summarizes wildcard use: use extends when you only produce values from a structure, and super when you only consume values into it, because a List of Number cannot accept a List of Integer as a subtype even though Integer is a subtype of Number. Type erasure means generic type arguments are removed at compile time, so a List of String and a List of Integer are the same class at runtime, you cannot overload methods that differ only by generic argument, and you cannot create arrays of a parameterized type directly. The compiler inserts casts and bridge methods so overriding still works after erasure, which is why reflection sometimes reveals synthetic bridge methods. When erasure loses information you need at runtime, pass an explicit Class token or a type token instead of fighting the type system.
followUps: Why can you not overload a method on List of String versus List of Integer?
How do you recover type information lost to erasure?
interviewQuestions.question: Explain PECS and type erasure, and the practical limits they place on generic code.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: PECS: extends for producers, super for consumers; erasure removes type arguments at runtime, so generic overloads and parameterized arrays are impossible and reflection may show bridge methods.
tips: Give one producer example and one consumer example.
Mention bridge methods — senior interviewers listen for them.
interviewQuestions.title: Generics: PECS and erasure

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: ConcurrentHashMap scales by striping locks across bins rather than locking the whole map, and its atomic bulk methods such as compute, merge, and forEach operate per bin, so they do not give you a consistent snapshot across the whole map. A mapping function in computeIfAbsent must be short, non-blocking, and side-effect free, because it can run while holding a bin lock and may be invoked more than once under contention, which can stall other threads or cause surprising duplicate work. Sizing matters less than in HashMap because concurrency level is a hint, not a hard segment count, but an undersized map still resizes under load, and a huge initial capacity wastes memory. For high-contention counters, prefer LongAdder over AtomicLong inside the map, and for compound multi-key updates, accept that you need an external lock or a redesign, not a single atomic map call.
followUps: Why is there no atomic operation across two keys?
When does LongAdder beat AtomicLong?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the scaling limits and traps of ConcurrentHashMap in high-contention code?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: It scales by bin-level locking, but compute functions run under a bin lock and may repeat, bulk operations are not whole-map atomic, and multi-key updates need external coordination.
tips: Name the computeIfAbsent trap specifically.
State plainly that no map call is atomic across two keys.
interviewQuestions.title: ConcurrentHashMap at scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A correct parallel reduction needs an associative, stateless combiner and an identity that is truly neutral, otherwise results vary between runs depending on how work is split. Stateful intermediate operations such as sorted, distinct, and limit on an unordered stream force buffering or coordination that can erase parallel gains, and encounter order adds further coordination costs that an unordered stream avoids. Short-circuiting operations such as findAny are faster in parallel than findFirst, which must respect order. Before parallelizing, check that the source splits efficiently — a LinkedList or an iterator-based stream splits poorly — that the per-element work is large enough to outweigh splitting overhead, and that no operation blocks or mutates shared state.
followUps: Why does a parallel reduce give different answers if the combiner is not associative?
Why is findAny faster than findFirst in parallel?
interviewQuestions.question: What makes a stream reduction correct in parallel, and which operations destroy parallel performance?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Parallel reduction needs an associative combiner and a true identity; stateful operations, encounter order, poor splitting, and blocking or mutating operations destroy its gains.
tips: Use associativity as the correctness test.
Mention findAny versus findFirst as the concrete ordering example.
interviewQuestions.title: Parallel stream correctness

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An executor saturates in stages: tasks queue up, threads grow to the maximum, the queue fills, and then the rejection policy decides whether callers block, run the task themselves, or drop it — and the default abort policy throws RejectedExecutionException at the worst moment. A bounded queue with caller-runs or a backpressure-aware policy protects downstream systems, while an unbounded queue hides overload until memory or latency explodes. Separate executors by workload class — CPU-bound, blocking I/O, and scheduled work — so one slow dependency cannot starve everything else, and expose queue depth, active threads, and rejections as metrics with alerts. Virtual threads change the calculus for blocking I/O by making a thread per task cheap, but they do not remove the need for bounds, timeouts, and backpressure when the downstream system itself is the bottleneck.
followUps: Why is an unbounded queue more dangerous than a rejection?
When do virtual threads not solve saturation?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design an executor so overload degrades gracefully instead of crashing the service?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Bound the queue, choose an explicit rejection policy, separate executors by workload, and alert on queue depth and rejections; virtual threads help blocking I/O but do not remove downstream limits.
tips: Walk through the saturation stages in order.
Warn that an unbounded queue hides overload until it is too late.
interviewQuestions.title: Executor saturation and backpressure

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start from the symptom: long pauses point to garbage collection logs and heap sizing, a steadily growing heap points to a leak, and high CPU without progress points to a hot loop or lock contention. Enable GC logging, then read pause times, allocation rate, and promotion rate before touching flags, and take a heap dump only after confirming the heap is actually growing, since a dump freezes or slows the process. Analyze the dump for the largest retained objects and their shortest paths to GC roots, which usually reveal a static cache, a listener never deregistered, or an unbounded collection. Metaspace growth points instead to classloader leaks, often from repeated redeploys, while native memory growth points outside the heap entirely. Fix the retention cause, then tune the collector; tuning flags around a leak only postpones the outage.
followUps: How do you distinguish a leak from a heap that is too small?
What does growth in Metaspace, rather than the heap, suggest?
interviewQuestions.question: Production heap usage climbs until the service restarts. How do you diagnose it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Confirm growth with GC logs, identify whether it is heap, Metaspace, or native memory, then analyze a heap dump for dominant retained objects and their paths to GC roots and fix the retention cause.
tips: Order the answer: confirm, locate, analyze, fix — not flags first.
Name the usual suspects: static caches, unremoved listeners, unbounded collections.
interviewQuestions.title: Diagnosing a production memory leak

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring AOP and @Transactional work through proxies: a call from outside the bean goes through the proxy, which starts a transaction or applies advice, while a call from one method of the bean to another bypasses the proxy entirely, so the annotation on the called method is silently ignored. The same applies to private methods, which proxies cannot intercept, and to final classes or methods with JDK dynamic proxies. The fixes are to restructure so the transactional method is called through another bean, to self-inject the proxy, or to use AspectJ weaving when proxy limits are truly unacceptable. This also explains why @Transactional on a method that only calls another method in the same class appears to do nothing, and why a rollback only happens for unchecked exceptions by default unless rollbackFor is configured.
followUps: Why does @Transactional not work on a private method?
How do you make a self-call go through the proxy?
interviewQuestions.question: Why does @Transactional sometimes silently do nothing, and how do proxies explain it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Proxies only intercept external calls, so self-invocation and private methods bypass @Transactional; call through another bean or the proxy, and remember rollback is unchecked-only by default.
tips: Explain the proxy mechanism before the fix.
Mention rollbackFor, since it is the second half of the same interview question.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring proxies and self-invocation

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Auto-configuration classes are ordered and conditional, so when two starters provide the same bean, the one whose conditions match and that is ordered first wins, and a user-defined bean of the same type normally makes auto-configuration back off via @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Conflicts usually come from an explicit @Bean that shadows the auto-configured one, a starter pulled in transitively that you did not expect, or a condition such as @ConditionalOnClass that behaves differently in tests versus production because the classpath differs. Debug with the auto-configuration report, which lists what applied, what was excluded, and why each candidate was skipped, and with the conditions evaluation report in tests. Prefer excluding a specific auto-configuration or defining a replacement bean deliberately over broad component-scan exclusions, which hide future surprises.
followUps: How do you find which starter brought in an unwanted bean?
When is excluding an auto-configuration better than overriding its bean?
interviewQuestions.question: Two starters configure the same bean and the wrong one wins. How do you diagnose and resolve it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Check conditions, ordering, and the auto-configuration report; a user bean normally backs auto-configuration off, so resolve conflicts by excluding a specific auto-configuration or defining the intended bean explicitly.
tips: Name the auto-configuration report as the first diagnostic step.
Distinguish transitive starter surprises from deliberate overrides.
interviewQuestions.title: Auto-configuration conflicts

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Filters run at the servlet level, before Spring MVC dispatches, so they see every request but not the handler, while interceptors run inside Spring MVC around the handler, with access to the controller method and model, and argument resolvers and exception resolvers run even closer to the handler. Use filters for cross-cutting transport concerns such as logging and authentication headers, interceptors for handler-aware concerns such as feature flags or tenant context, and @ControllerAdvice for consistent error translation. For asynchronous handling, Callable and DeferredResult release the request thread while work completes, and WebFlux-style reactive endpoints only help when the whole downstream chain is non-blocking; wrapping a blocking call in a reactive type just moves the blockage. Idempotency for retried POSTs belongs at the API layer with an idempotency key stored with the result, not in the client retry logic alone.
followUps: Why can a filter not know which controller will handle a request?
When does async handling not improve throughput?
interviewQuestions.question: How do filters, interceptors, and async handling differ in Spring MVC, and where does idempotency belong?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Filters run before dispatch without handler knowledge, interceptors run around the handler, async releases the request thread, and idempotency belongs server-side with a stored key and result.
tips: Order the layers from outermost to innermost.
Flag wrapping a blocking call in a reactive type as fake async.
interviewQuestions.title: Filters, interceptors, and async MVC

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Optimistic locking with a @Version column lets concurrent updates proceed and fails the loser with an OptimisticLockException instead of silently overwriting, which suits low-contention data such as user profiles, while pessimistic locking suits high-contention resources such as inventory counts. Isolation levels trade correctness for concurrency: read committed prevents dirty reads, repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads, and serializable prevents phantoms, but each stronger level costs throughput and increases lock waits. Lost updates, phantom reads, and write skew are the anomalies to name, and the fix is usually a version column plus a retry for the loser, or a pessimistic lock for the contested row, rather than raising the global isolation level. Second-level caching helps read-heavy reference data but can serve stale entities across nodes, so it needs explicit invalidation and must never cache frequently mutated data.
followUps: When would you choose pessimistic over optimistic locking?
Why is raising the global isolation level usually the wrong fix?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle concurrent updates in JPA, and what do isolation levels actually buy you?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Optimistic locking with @Version for low contention, pessimistic locks for hot rows, and isolation levels chosen per anomaly, not raised globally; cache only stable reference data.
tips: Pair each locking strategy with its contention profile.
Name one anomaly per isolation level instead of reciting definitions.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA locking and isolation

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Two-phase commit gives strong consistency across services but couples them to a coordinator and blocks on coordinator failure, so most systems accept eventual consistency and design for it. A saga sequences local transactions with compensating actions for rollback, but compensations are not true rollbacks: they are new business operations that must themselves be idempotent and must handle partial failure. The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem by writing the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change, then relaying it asynchronously, so an event is never lost and never sent without its state change. Consumers must still be idempotent, because at-least-once delivery means duplicates are normal, and event schemas must evolve compatibly so old consumers keep working.
followUps: Why is a compensating action not the same as a rollback?
How does the outbox pattern solve the dual-write problem?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you keep data consistent across microservices without distributed transactions?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use sagas with idempotent compensations for multi-service workflows and the transactional outbox for reliable event publication, and make every consumer idempotent under at-least-once delivery.
tips: Contrast 2PC blocking with saga compensation explicitly.
Name the dual-write problem — it is the heart of the question.
interviewQuestions.title: Sagas and the transactional outbox

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and running totals compute over a window of rows without collapsing them, so you can rank orders per customer or compute a moving average while keeping every row. Offset pagination with LIMIT and OFFSET is simple but scans and discards skipped rows, so it slows as the offset grows and can skip or repeat rows when data changes between pages. Keyset pagination, filtering on an ordered unique key such as a timestamp plus id, stays fast at any depth and is stable under inserts, but it cannot jump to an arbitrary page number. Covering indexes, which include every column a query needs, let the database answer from the index alone, but each extra index costs write performance and storage, so verify with the execution plan and measure on realistic data volumes.
followUps: Why can offset pagination skip rows when data changes?
When is a covering index worth its write cost?
interviewQuestions.question: When do window functions and keyset pagination beat GROUP BY and OFFSET pagination?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Window functions rank and aggregate without collapsing rows; keyset pagination on an ordered unique key stays fast and stable at depth, while OFFSET scans skipped rows and shifts under concurrent writes.
tips: Give one window-function example and one keyset example.
State the OFFSET weakness in terms of scanning, not just slowness.
interviewQuestions.title: Window functions and keyset pagination

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The task is to design an LRU cache with get and put in constant time. The idiomatic approach pairs a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency: the map gives constant-time lookup, and the list lets you move a node to the front on access and evict the tail node on overflow, both in constant time. On get, return the value and move its node to the front; on put, insert or update the node, move it to the front, and if the size exceeds capacity, remove the tail node from both the list and the map. A linked hash map in access-order mode provides this out of the box in Java, but interviewers usually want the map-plus-list structure explained, and for a concurrent version you must add locking or sharding rather than assuming the structure is thread-safe.
followUps: How would you make this cache thread-safe?
How does the design change if eviction must consider entry size, not just count?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: design an LRU cache with constant-time get and put. What data structures do you combine, and why?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Combine a hash map for constant-time lookup with a doubly linked list for recency order: move accessed nodes to the front and evict from the tail.
tips: Explain why each structure alone is insufficient.
Mention LinkedHashMap access-order mode, then explain the underlying structure anyway.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: LRU cache design

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: First, establish whether threads are blocked, deadlocked, or merely busy: thread dumps taken a few seconds apart show threads stuck in the same place for a deadlock or lock wait, versus threads moving through different code for CPU saturation. A common root cause is a thread pool exhausted by calls to a slow downstream service without timeouts, so every request thread waits and new requests queue until the service appears dead. Mitigate immediately by shedding load or restarting with bounded pools and timeouts, then fix the dependency contract: add timeouts, bulkheads per dependency, and circuit breakers, and alert on queue depth before it reaches saturation. A post-incident review should ask why the missing timeout was not caught by a checklist or test, because the same failure will recur with the next slow dependency.
followUps: How do thread dumps distinguish deadlock from CPU saturation?
What metric would have warned you before saturation?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: a service stops responding under normal traffic, CPU is low, and restarts only help briefly. How do you diagnose it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Low CPU plus unresponsiveness suggests thread-pool exhaustion or deadlock; compare thread dumps over time, then bound pools, add timeouts and bulkheads, and alert on queue depth.
tips: Use the low-CPU clue — it rules out a hot loop.
Name bulkheads as the structural fix, not just timeouts.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: thread-pool exhaustion

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Records give concise immutable data carriers with automatically generated equals, hashCode, and accessors, and they suit DTOs and value objects, but they are final and cannot extend another class, so they are a poor fit for entities with evolving behaviour or frameworks that require proxies and no-arg construction. Sealed classes restrict which classes may extend them, which makes a hierarchy exhaustive and lets pattern-matching switches be checked by the compiler, and pattern matching replaces chains of instanceof checks and casts with a single readable form. Virtual threads make a thread-per-request style cheap for blocking I/O workloads, but they do not help CPU-bound work and they can pin a carrier thread when code synchronizes on a monitor. Migrate incrementally: introduce records and pattern matching where they clarify code, and adopt virtual threads only after confirming the workload is blocking I/O and the libraries used do not pin carriers.
followUps: Why are records a poor fit for JPA entities?
When does a virtual thread pin its carrier thread?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide where records, sealed classes, pattern matching, and virtual threads actually help?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Records for immutable data carriers, sealed classes for exhaustive hierarchies, pattern matching for type dispatch, and virtual threads only for blocking I/O workloads that do not pin carriers.
tips: Give one good fit and one poor fit per feature.
Warn about carrier pinning for virtual threads — it is the current senior-level trap.
interviewQuestions.title: Modern Java: where each feature fits

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: API evolution is a compatibility contract, not just a code change: adding a method to an interface breaks existing implementors, changing a return type or generic signature breaks callers, and renaming a public type breaks everyone, so stable APIs evolve by addition and deprecation, not by modification. A plugin or extension architecture should therefore depend on narrow, versioned interfaces, use composition over inheritance so hosts are not coupled to plugin internals, and isolate plugins with their own classloaders when versions of a shared library must coexist. Reflection and serialization bypass normal access rules and type checks, so they belong at system boundaries with explicit schemas and validation, not scattered through business logic. When a breaking change is unavoidable, ship it behind a new major version with a migration guide, dual support during transition, and telemetry showing the old API is actually unused before removal.
followUps: Why does adding a method to an interface break implementors?
When is a classloader boundary worth its complexity?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design a public Java API and plugin system that can evolve without breaking its consumers?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Evolve by addition and deprecation, depend on narrow versioned interfaces, isolate plugins by classloader when needed, and remove old APIs only after telemetry proves they are unused.
tips: Frame compatibility as a contract, not a preference.
Name the interface-addition breakage — it is the classic trap.
interviewQuestions.title: API evolution and plugin design

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: At moderate scale the right collection is usually obvious, but at large scale the choice is driven by access pattern, memory overhead, and allocation behaviour, not by asymptotic complexity alone. An ArrayList of boxed objects costs far more memory and GC pressure than a primitive array or a specialized collection, a HashMap with a poor hash function degrades under adversarial keys, and a concurrent structure with high contention can be slower than a sharded or thread-local design. For ordered data, a balanced tree gives logarithmic ordered operations that a hash map cannot, and for streaming aggregation, a purpose-built accumulator avoids building intermediate collections entirely. The senior answer quantifies: estimate element count, per-element overhead, read-to-write ratio, and contention, then measure with a realistic workload, because a choice that is correct at ten thousand elements can be wrong at ten million.
followUps: When does a HashMap lose to a tree or a sorted array?
How do boxed primitives change the memory math?
interviewQuestions.question: How does collection choice change when a data structure must hold tens of millions of entries?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Beyond asymptotic complexity, decide on memory overhead, allocation and GC pressure, hash quality, ordering needs, and contention, and measure at realistic scale.
tips: Quantify: element count, overhead, read-write ratio, contention.
Name boxing overhead as the hidden cost most candidates miss.
interviewQuestions.title: Collections at scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Streams excel at declarative, in-memory transformation of finite data, but they are a poor fit for infinite or backpressured sources, for operations that need early exit with complex state, and for pipelines where checked exceptions or resource cleanup must be precise. A reactive stream, by contrast, models asynchronous data flow with demand signalling, so a slow consumer can slow the producer instead of being overwhelmed by an unbounded buffer. Mixing the two naively — collecting a reactive source into a list just to stream it, or blocking inside a reactive pipeline — loses the benefits of both. Choose plain streams for bounded in-memory work, reactive streams for asynchronous event flows with backpressure, and plain loops when the logic is stateful, exception-heavy, or performance-critical enough that stream overhead and boxing matter.
followUps: What does backpressure protect against that a plain stream cannot?
When is a plain loop better than a stream?
interviewQuestions.question: When should you not use Java Streams, and how does reactive streaming differ?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Streams suit bounded in-memory transformation; reactive streams add demand signalling for async flows, and plain loops win for stateful, exception-heavy, or allocation-sensitive code.
tips: Define backpressure in one sentence before comparing.
Give a concrete anti-pattern: collecting a reactive source just to re-stream it.
interviewQuestions.title: Streams versus reactive streams

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Lock-free algorithms use atomic compare-and-swap loops instead of locks, so a thread that fails a CAS retries rather than blocking, which avoids deadlock and keeps progress even when some threads stall, but retries under contention can burn CPU and the ABA problem can make a changed-then-restored value look unchanged. False sharing is the subtler trap: two threads updating different variables that share a cache line force the line to bounce between cores, so padding or grouping hot fields apart can yield large speedups in counters and queues. Distributed locking adds another layer: a lock held in Redis or a database must have a lease with expiry, a fencing token to reject stale holders after a pause, and a design that tolerates the lock holder dying, because a lock without expiry becomes a permanent outage. Prefer lock-free structures for single-JVM hot paths, and treat distributed locks as a coordination mechanism of last resort, with idempotent work underneath.
followUps: What is the ABA problem in a CAS loop?
Why does a distributed lock need a fencing token?
interviewQuestions.question: When do lock-free algorithms and distributed locks help, and what are their traps?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Lock-free CAS avoids blocking but risks retry storms and ABA; false sharing punishes nearby hot fields; distributed locks need leases and fencing tokens and should sit above idempotent work.
tips: Pair each technique with its specific trap.
Mention fencing tokens — they separate experienced answers from textbook ones.
interviewQuestions.title: Lock-free and distributed locking

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Low-latency collectors such as ZGC and Shenandoah keep pauses in the low milliseconds by doing most work concurrently with the application, at the cost of higher CPU overhead and throughput loss compared with G1 or Parallel. Tuning starts from a latency budget and a measurement: GC logs showing pause distribution, allocation rate, and heap occupancy, plus application latency percentiles, because average pause alone hides the tail that users feel. Escape analysis and JIT inlining reduce allocation in hot code, but they cannot rescue a design that allocates heavily per request, so the first optimization is usually fewer allocations, not more flags. For very large heaps or strict latency targets, evaluate the concurrent collector under production-like load and accept its CPU cost deliberately; for batch or throughput workloads, that trade is usually wrong.
followUps: Why is average GC pause a misleading metric?
When is a low-latency collector the wrong choice?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose and tune a garbage collector for a strict latency target?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Start from a latency budget and percentile measurements; ZGC and Shenandoah buy millisecond pauses with CPU overhead, so use them for latency-sensitive services and reduce allocation before tuning flags.
tips: Insist on percentiles, not averages.
State the throughput cost explicitly — it is a trade, not a free win.
interviewQuestions.title: Low-latency GC tuning

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Circular dependencies are usually a design smell: two beans needing each other at construction time means their responsibilities are tangled, and the honest fix is to extract the shared logic into a third bean or to invert the dependency. Spring can paper over some cycles with setter injection or proxies, but constructor injection rightly fails fast on a cycle, and suppressing that failure hides the design problem while making startup order fragile. Startup time in a large context comes from eager singleton creation, classpath scanning, and auto-configuration evaluation, so the remedies are lazy initialization for genuinely optional beans, narrower component scans, and fewer, more deliberate auto-configurations, measured with startup reports rather than guessed. For a modular monolith, enforce module boundaries with package rules and internal-only APIs, so the monolith stays decomposable instead of becoming a distributed monolith in disguise.
followUps: Why does constructor injection fail fast on a cycle while setter injection does not?
How do you keep a modular monolith decomposable?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle circular dependencies and slow startup in a large Spring application?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Treat cycles as a design smell to refactor, not to suppress; constructor injection failing fast is a feature, and startup improves with lazy beans, narrow scans, and measured auto-configuration costs.
tips: Take a position: refactor the cycle, do not work around it.
Mention package-boundary rules for modular monoliths.
interviewQuestions.title: Circular dependencies and startup time

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A custom starter should be a thin, opinionated packaging of auto-configuration, default properties, and dependencies, with every bean conditional so applications can override it, and with its own configuration properties namespace so settings do not collide. Multi-tenancy belongs in explicit layers: tenant resolution from a header or token, tenant-scoped data source routing or schema selection, and tenant context propagation through async boundaries, with tests that run the same scenario under two tenants. Observability is part of the starter contract: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics for the operations the starter performs, and health indicators that fail meaningfully rather than always reporting up. Graceful shutdown matters equally: stop accepting new work, drain in-flight requests within a timeout, and only then close resources, so rolling deploys do not drop requests.
followUps: How do you propagate tenant context across async boundaries?
What makes a health indicator meaningful rather than decorative?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you build a reusable Spring Boot starter for a multi-tenant platform?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Keep starters thin and conditional with their own properties namespace, resolve tenant explicitly and propagate it through async work, and include observability and graceful shutdown as part of the contract.
tips: List the starter contract: conditional beans, namespace, observability, shutdown.
Name tenant propagation across async boundaries as the hard part.
interviewQuestions.title: Custom starters and multi-tenancy

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: API versioning is a compatibility strategy, not a URL prefix: version in the URI for coarse, client-visible breaking changes, in headers or content negotiation when clients can handle it, and prefer backwards-compatible evolution — additive fields, optional parameters, and tolerant readers — so most changes need no version at all. Contract tests, where consumers publish the expectations they rely on, catch breaking changes before release far more reliably than manual coordination, and a deprecation policy with sunset headers and usage telemetry tells you when an old version can actually be retired. Rate limiting and request validation belong at the gateway or filter layer for coarse protection, with fine-grained business limits in the service layer where domain context lives. Never version by forking controller code without a shared core, or the versions will drift and a bug fix will land in one version only.
followUps: When can you avoid versioning entirely?
How do you know when an old API version is safe to retire?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you version a public API and retire old versions without breaking clients?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Prefer backwards-compatible evolution, version coarsely when breaking, enforce compatibility with consumer contract tests, and retire versions only on telemetry plus a published sunset policy.
tips: Lead with backwards-compatible evolution, not versioning schemes.
Name consumer contract tests as the enforcement mechanism.
interviewQuestions.title: API versioning and contract tests

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: JPA excels at single-database domain modelling, but it strains at scale in three places: a single write database becomes a bottleneck, a shared entity graph couples read and write shapes, and lazy loading plus the persistence context add overhead to bulk work. The standard responses are read replicas for read-heavy workloads with explicit tolerance for replication lag, CQRS read models that precompute the shapes queries actually need, and bulk operations through JDBC or batch statements that bypass the persistence context for imports and updates. Sharding is a last resort, not a first step, because it breaks joins, transactions, and reporting across shards and forces application-level routing and rebalancing. The senior judgement is knowing which scale problem you actually have — read volume, write volume, or data volume — because each has a different remedy.
followUps: When does a read replica hurt rather than help?
Why is sharding a last resort?
interviewQuestions.question: Where does JPA break down at scale, and what replaces each piece?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use read replicas for read volume, CQRS read models for mismatched read shapes, and JDBC batching for bulk work; reserve sharding for data volume it alone can solve, since it breaks joins and transactions.
tips: Diagnose the scale problem first: reads, writes, or data volume.
Warn that replication lag makes replicas unsuitable for read-after-write flows.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA at scale: replicas, CQRS, sharding

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Event-driven architecture decouples producers from consumers in time and in topology, but it trades immediate consistency for eventual consistency, and that trade must be visible in the product: user interfaces need pending states, and business processes need compensations for late or failed events. Schema evolution is the long-term cost, so events should be versioned, backwards-compatible, and self-describing, with consumers tolerating unknown fields and producers never reusing a field name for a new meaning. Every consumer must be idempotent with a stored record of processed event ids, because at-least-once delivery guarantees duplicates, and every event flow needs dead-letter handling, replay capability, and distributed tracing across producer and consumer. If a workflow needs an immediate, synchronous answer, an event is the wrong tool — use a request-response call and reserve events for facts other services react to.
followUps: How do you make an event consumer safe to replay?
When is an event the wrong choice versus a synchronous call?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design an event-driven system that survives duplicates, schema changes, and failures?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Design for eventual consistency with pending states and compensations, version events compatibly, make consumers idempotent, and provide dead-letter handling, replay, and end-to-end tracing.
tips: Name the product consequence of eventual consistency, not just the pattern.
Insist on stored processed-event ids for idempotency.
interviewQuestions.title: Event-driven architecture at scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: At very large tables, query design is index design: range queries need the range column last in a composite index after equality columns, selective filters beat broad ones, and sorting without an index forces a costly sort of the full result. Partitioning by a natural key such as time lets old partitions be archived or dropped cheaply and keeps working sets small, but queries that do not filter on the partition key must scan every partition. Locking behaviour matters as much as speed: long transactions hold locks and block writers, gap locks under repeatable read can deadlock concurrent inserts, and the remedy is usually shorter transactions, consistent lock ordering, and retrying deadlocked transactions rather than raising timeouts. Always verify with the execution plan on production-sized data, because a plan that is fine at a million rows can be catastrophic at a hundred million.
followUps: Why should the range column come last in a composite index?
How do you reduce deadlocks without raising timeouts?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design indexes, partitioning, and transactions for tables with hundreds of millions of rows?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Order composite indexes equality-first and range-last, partition on the key queries actually filter by, keep transactions short with consistent lock ordering, and verify plans at production scale.
tips: Give the composite-index ordering rule concretely.
Name gap locks as the deadlock mechanism, not just deadlocks in general.
interviewQuestions.title: SQL at very large scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The task is to design a rate limiter that works across multiple service instances. The idiomatic approach is a token-bucket or fixed-window counter per key, stored in a shared store with an atomic increment and expiry, so every instance observes the same count. A single-instance in-memory limiter is correct only until the second instance deploys, at which point each instance enforces its own limit and the effective limit multiplies. For strict fairness, use a shared atomic counter with a window, accept the small race window of fixed windows or the complexity of a sliding-window log, and return a standard too-many-requests response with a retry-after hint. Edge cases to name are clock skew between instances, hot keys that concentrate on one store shard, and the failure mode when the store itself is unavailable — fail open for non-critical endpoints, fail closed for abuse-sensitive ones.
followUps: Why does a per-instance limiter break when you scale out?
Should the limiter fail open or fail closed when its store is down?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: design a rate limiter that stays correct when the service scales to many instances. What is your approach?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a shared atomic counter per key with a window in a central store, such as a token bucket, so all instances share one limit; per-instance counters multiply the limit on scale-out.
tips: Start from the scale-out failure of in-memory limiters.
Name the fail-open versus fail-closed decision for store outages.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: distributed rate limiter

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Apply the strangler pattern: put the new service behind the existing monolith's interface, route a slice of traffic or a single capability to it, and expand slice by slice, so every step is reversible and the old system remains the fallback. Data is the hard part: keep a single source of truth during transition, synchronize with change-data-capture or dual writes guarded by reconciliation jobs, and migrate data in small, verifiable batches with checksums rather than one big cutover. Rollback means routing traffic back and reconciling any writes the new service made, which only works if writes are idempotent and the old system can still accept them, so design the new service's writes with that constraint from day one. Success criteria are not the migration itself but the metrics that prove it: error rates, latency, and data-consistency checks at each slice, with a named owner and a decision point for each expansion.
followUps: Why is a big-bang cutover riskier than strangler migration?
How do you reconcile data written by the new service during rollback?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: you must extract a payment capability from a monolith into a service without downtime. How do you plan it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Strangle it slice by slice behind the old interface, keep one source of truth with reconciled synchronization, migrate data in verifiable batches, and make rollback possible via idempotent writes.
tips: Lead with the strangler pattern and reversibility.
Name data reconciliation, not just traffic routing, as the hard part.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: strangler migration

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: First, establish scope and reversibility: confirm the regression with a controlled comparison, such as canary traffic on the old and new versions under the same load, and check whether the change is the JDK, a library upgrade shipped with it, or a configuration change that rode along. Then narrow with evidence in order: GC logs and pause percentiles, JIT compilation and deoptimization logs, thread and CPU profiles, and dependency changelogs, looking for a behaviour change in a collector, a hashing order, or a default that the application silently depended on. As a staff-level decision, you would halt the rollout at the canary stage, keep the old version deployable, and choose between pinning the old version, tuning the new one, or fixing the application assumption, based on which evidence you have and how long each path takes. The post-incident action is a regression gate: a performance benchmark and a canary comparison in the upgrade pipeline, so the next JDK upgrade cannot regress silently.
followUps: How do you separate a JDK regression from a library or config change shipped with it?
When do you roll back versus tune forward?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: after a JDK upgrade, latency percentiles regress in production. As the technical lead, how do you investigate and decide?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Compare canary versions under identical load, narrow with GC, JIT, and profile evidence, halt the rollout, and decide between rollback, tuning, or fixing the app assumption based on evidence and time to fix.
tips: Lead with the canary comparison, not with a guess about the collector.
Frame the decision explicitly: rollback, tune, or fix — with criteria.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: JDK upgrade regression
