practiceItems.description: ServiceA depends on ServiceB and ServiceB depends on ServiceA. The application fails to start with a circular reference error. How do you fix it properly, rather than just working around the error?
practiceItems.solution: First question whether the cycle is real: often one direction can be removed by extracting the shared logic into a third service both depend on, or by having one side depend on an event or interface instead of the concrete class. If a cycle is genuinely needed, inject one side lazily with @Lazy, or restructure so the shared behaviour lives in a separate bean. Avoid re-enabling circular references via spring.main.allow-circular-references as a permanent fix, since it hides a design problem and can leave partially-initialized beans.
practiceItems.title: Fixing a circular bean dependency

practiceItems.description: A report generator builds a large CSV by concatenating strings with + inside a loop over 100,000 rows, and it is very slow with high memory churn. Diagnose the cause and propose a fix.
practiceItems.solution: Because String is immutable, each + creates a new string and copies all previous content, giving quadratic copying and heavy garbage collection. Replace the loop body with a single StringBuilder created before the loop, append each row, and call toString() once at the end. For joining with a delimiter, StringJoiner or String.join / Collectors.joining are idiomatic alternatives.
practiceItems.title: Slow string building in a loop

practiceItems.description: A REST endpoint accepts a registration request and manually checks each field with if statements scattered through the service layer. Invalid data sometimes reaches the database. How would you restructure validation?
practiceItems.solution: Validate at the API boundary with Bean Validation: annotate the request DTO with constraints such as @NotBlank, @Email and @Size, add @Valid on the controller parameter, and handle failures centrally in a @ControllerAdvice that returns 400 with per-field errors. Keep business-rule checks (for example, whether an email is already registered) in the service layer, and keep the DTO separate from the entity so validation rules do not leak into persistence.
practiceItems.title: Validating a REST request

practiceItems.description: A service depends on a repository and an external client. The team writes only slow end-to-end tests, so feedback is slow and failures are hard to localize. Propose a testing approach for this service.
practiceItems.solution: Test the service in isolation as a unit test with the repository and client mocked (for example with Mockito), covering success, not-found and error paths quickly. Add a separate slice test (such as @DataJpaTest) for the repository's real queries, and a small number of end-to-end tests for the critical happy path only. Log with a correlation id so a failure in any layer can be traced, and keep test data builders so tests stay readable as cases grow.
practiceItems.title: Choosing a test for a service

practiceItems.explanation: Count++ is read-modify-write, so two threads can read the same value and both write back the same incremented value, losing one update. volatile only guarantees visibility of the latest write, not atomicity of a compound action. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is atomic, and a lock would also work.
options: volatile makes count++ atomic.
The JVM reorders the loop body.
Two threads can interleave the read, increment and write of count++, losing an update.
AtomicInteger is slower, so the JVM skips updates.
practiceItems.prompt: A shared int counter incremented by two threads with volatile ends up below the expected total. Why?
practiceItems.title: Lost update with volatile

practiceItems.explanation: A fixed pool of 2 threads with an unbounded queue will accept tasks forever, so a burst can queue millions of tasks and exhaust memory. A bounded queue plus an explicit rejection policy (abort, caller-runs, or discard) makes overload visible and bounded. More threads alone only moves the bottleneck; shutting down the pool after submit is not a sizing fix.
options: Use a cached thread pool instead.
Increase the pool to 200 threads.
Use a bounded work queue with an explicit rejection policy, so overload is bounded and visible.
Submit tasks with invokeAll instead of submit.
practiceItems.prompt: A fixed pool of 2 threads with an unbounded queue runs out of memory under a burst of tasks. What is the best fix?
practiceItems.title: Executor queue sizing

practiceItems.explanation: The young generation is collected frequently and cheaply because most objects die young (the weak generational hypothesis); surviving objects are promoted to the old generation, which is collected rarely and more expensively. Tenuring thresholds control how many young collections an object survives before promotion.
options: Objects are allocated in the old generation first.
Most objects die young, so the young generation is collected often and cheaply, and survivors are promoted.
The young generation is never collected.
Promotion happens on every method call.
practiceItems.prompt: Why does the JVM split the heap into a young and an old generation?
practiceItems.title: Generational garbage collection

practiceItems.explanation: A JWT is signed, so the server can verify it without storing session state, but its claims cannot be changed after signing — the token stays valid until it expires. That is why access tokens are kept short-lived and revocation is handled by expiry plus refresh-token rotation, a denylist, or a version claim, rather than by editing the token.
options: Delete the token from the database.
You cannot edit a signed token; you must wait for expiry or use short lifetimes plus a revocation mechanism such as refresh rotation or a denylist.
Change the signing key for just that user.
Send the token a logout request.
practiceItems.prompt: A user's JWT must be invalidated immediately after logout. Why is this not as simple as deleting a session?
practiceItems.title: JWT revocation

practiceItems.explanation: Accessing a lazily loaded association after the persistence context (EntityManager / transaction) has closed throws LazyInitializationException, because there is no session left to fetch the data. Fetching the needed data inside the transaction with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph, or mapping to a DTO inside the transaction, fixes it. Open Session in View hides the problem by keeping the session open into the view layer, at the cost of unpredictable queries.
options: The entity has no default constructor.
The lazy association is accessed after the persistence context has closed.
The association is annotated fetch = EAGER.
The query used a DTO projection.
practiceItems.prompt: What causes LazyInitializationException?
practiceItems.title: LazyInitializationException

practiceItems.explanation: A circuit breaker stops calling a failing downstream service after a threshold, fails fast, and periodically lets a trial call through to check recovery. Retrying immediately and forever amplifies the overload; adding threads only delays saturation; caching only helps if stale data is acceptable for that endpoint.
options: Retry every failed call immediately and indefinitely.
Increase the caller thread pool until the downstream recovers.
Trip a circuit breaker: fail fast after a failure threshold and probe periodically for recovery.
Cache every response permanently.
practiceItems.prompt: Service A calls a failing Service B, and retries pile up until A also collapses. Which pattern prevents this cascade?
practiceItems.title: Circuit breaker

Buffered streams batch small reads and writes into fewer system calls.
Buffered streams make files thread-safe.
Buffered streams load the entire file into memory.

practiceItems.title: Buffered I/O

practiceItems.title: Happens-before

practiceItems.title: Stop-the-world pauses

practiceItems.description: Two threads each transfer money between the same two accounts, but in opposite directions, and the program sometimes hangs forever. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix that preserves correctness.
practiceItems.solution: This is deadlock: each thread holds one account's lock and waits for the other's. Fix it by imposing a single global lock order — for example, always lock the account with the smaller id first — so no thread can hold one lock while waiting for a lock another thread holds in the opposite order. Alternatives include using one lock per transfer operation, or tryLock with a timeout and retry, but a consistent lock order is the cleanest fix. Also verify with thread dumps that the hang is a lock cycle, not an infinite loop.
practiceItems.title: Deadlock in account transfers

practiceItems.description: A latency-sensitive service suffers periodic 2-second pauses, and GC logs show long old-generation collections. How do you investigate and reduce the pauses without guessing at flags?
practiceItems.solution: First confirm GC is the cause: enable GC logging (for example -Xlog:gc*) and correlate pause timestamps with the latency spikes. Then check what is being promoted: look for large short-lived allocations, oversized caches, or objects surviving because of long-lived references. Reduce allocation (reuse buffers, avoid boxing in hot paths, cap caches) before tuning the collector. If pauses remain, try a low-pause collector such as G1 with a pause-time goal or ZGC, and measure throughput and pause percentiles before and after — a collector change that fixes p99 at the cost of unacceptable throughput is not a win.
practiceItems.title: Diagnosing long GC pauses

practiceItems.description: A single-page app stores a long-lived JWT in localStorage and calls APIs with it. After a token theft incident, the team must redesign token handling. What should change, and what should stay?
practiceItems.solution: Move to short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus rotating refresh tokens: each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token is detected on reuse and the whole token family can be revoked. Store the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie rather than localStorage where JavaScript can read it, and keep the short-lived access token in memory. Never put passwords, roles that must be revocable, or other sensitive data in the JWT payload, since it is only base64-encoded. Add a server-side revocation list or token version for immediate logout of compromised accounts.
practiceItems.title: Redesigning JWT handling after theft

practiceItems.description: A controller returns a JPA entity directly. The JSON serializer touches a lazily loaded collection and the request fails with LazyInitializationException in production but not in tests. Explain the difference and propose a fix.
practiceItems.solution: In tests the transaction (or Open Session in View) is often still open when serialization happens, so lazy loading succeeds; in production the transaction has closed before the serializer runs. Fix it properly: fetch exactly what the response needs inside the transaction — a JOIN FETCH query, an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection — and return a DTO, not the entity. That also prevents leaking internal fields and accidental extra queries. Do not fix it by marking the association EAGER or by enabling Open Session in View in production, both of which hide the problem and cause unpredictable queries.
practiceItems.title: LazyInitializationException in production only

practiceItems.description: Checkout calls inventory, payment and notification services in sequence. When payment is slow, checkout threads block, timeouts cascade, and one slow service takes down the whole checkout flow. Propose a resilient design using timeouts, bulkheads and observability.
practiceItems.solution: Give every downstream call an explicit timeout (shorter than the caller's own timeout) so a slow service fails fast instead of holding threads. Isolate each dependency with a bulkhead — a dedicated thread pool or concurrency limit — so payment slowness cannot exhaust the pool used for inventory. Add a circuit breaker so repeated failures fail fast and recover gradually, and retry only idempotent calls with backoff and a cap. Make payment calls idempotent with an idempotency key so a retried request cannot double-charge. Expose health, metrics and traces (via Actuator and distributed tracing) so the slow dependency is visible before it cascades, and design the checkout to degrade gracefully — for example, queue the notification instead of blocking checkout on it.
practiceItems.title: Resilient checkout across microservices

options: The Situation, so the interviewer understands all the background.
The Action, because it is the evidence of what you personally did.
The Result, because outcomes matter more than process.
The Task, because your job title explains your seniority.

practiceItems.prompt: What do the four letters of STAR stand for?

practiceItems.description: A candidate answers 'Tell me about a time you handled a tight deadline' like this: 'We had a really busy period at work and everyone was stressed. The project was complicated and there were lots of stakeholders. We worked really hard and in the end we managed to deliver it, which was great.' Evaluate this answer and rewrite it into a strong STAR answer (use a clearly fictional scenario).
practiceItems.solution: Weaknesses: no specific situation, no personal task or role ('we' throughout), no concrete actions ('worked really hard' is not a step), and no measurable result. A strong rewrite: Situation — a fictional reporting tool had to launch in two weeks when its data source changed format. Task — the candidate owned the data-import part. Action — mapped the format differences, proposed a translation layer instead of rewriting every report, built it behind a flag, and compared old and new outputs on sample data. Result — launched on the original date with matching outputs, and the translation layer made the next format change take hours instead of days. Lesson: check external source stability early in planning.

A failure where the outcome was partial but the lesson is concrete.
A 'failure' that is secretly a strength, such as working too hard or caring too much.
A failure in which you misjudged a situation and explain what you would do differently.

practiceItems.description: A candidate answers a conflict question by spending most of the answer explaining why their teammate's approach was wrong and how the candidate eventually proved them wrong. Improve this answer: what should change in tone, structure, and ending?
practiceItems.solution: Change the tone: describe the disagreement as a difference in view or priority, not as the teammate being wrong, and avoid blame or gossip. Change the structure: show listening first (what the teammate's concern was and why it was reasonable), then the discussion, then how a decision was reached. Change the ending: close with the resolution and the working relationship afterwards, plus what the candidate changed about how they handle disagreements — not with a victory lap.

The problem the project solved, and for whom.
A detailed description of the database schema.
A list of every feature the project shipped.

Purpose and users, components and request flow, data and storage, scale and failure.
Framework choices first, then purpose, then failure modes.
The hardest bug first, then the overall architecture.

practiceItems.description: An interviewer asks: 'What happens when your notification service goes down?' A candidate replies: 'It never goes down; we built it well.' Rewrite this into a strong deep-dive answer using a fictional booking system where notifications are sent asynchronously from a queue.
practiceItems.solution: A strong answer: bookings still succeed because the notification worker reads from a queue and is separate from the booking path, so a worker outage delays messages rather than losing bookings. On recovery, queued notifications are retried and delivered. Detection comes from queue-depth and worker-health alerts. The deliberate trade-off: delaying an email was judged acceptable, losing a booking was not. If the queue itself failed, bookings would still be recorded but notifications would need a replay from booking records — that is the residual risk, and it is why queue durability was chosen over speed.

practiceItems.description: A colleague proposes a sliding-window solution for finding the shortest subarray with sum at least K, but the array may contain negative numbers. Evaluate the proposal and describe a correct approach.
practiceItems.solution: The proposal is incorrect: the sliding-window shrink step relies on the sum only decreasing when an element is removed, which fails with negative numbers, because removing a negative element increases the sum and a window that currently fails could succeed after growing further. A correct approach uses prefix sums with a map from prefix value to earliest index, or, for the general case with arbitrary values, a monotonic deque over prefix sums (the standard solution for shortest subarray with sum at least K). State the assumption explicitly: sliding window for sum constraints requires non-negative numbers.
practiceItems.title: Sliding window with negative numbers

practiceItems.description: You need a leaderboard supporting frequent score updates, lookups of a player's score, and listing the top 10 players. Which structures would you combine, and what are the complexities?
practiceItems.solution: Use a HashMap from player to score for O(1) average lookup and update, combined with a structure for ranking. For top 10 only, a min-heap of size 10 rebuilt or maintained on updates gives O(log 10), effectively constant, per update in the simple rebuild approach, or maintain a TreeMap from score to players for O(log n) updates and O(10) top-10 reads. Avoid re-sorting all players on every update, which is O(n log n) per update, and avoid a plain list scan for lookups, which is O(n).
practiceItems.title: Choosing a structure for a leaderboard

practiceItems.explanation: Strict equality (===) compares type and value without coercion, so number 1 is not equal to string "1". Loose equality (==) coerces the string to a number, so it returns true. The other options get at least one comparison wrong, which is why preferring === avoids this whole class of surprise.
options: true and true
false and true
false and false
true and false
practiceItems.prompt: What is the result of 1 === "1" and 1 == "1" in JavaScript?
practiceItems.title: Strict versus loose equality

practiceItems.explanation: A closure keeps its enclosing scope alive: the inner function retains a reference to the variable, not a copy, so increments persist across calls. It is not destroyed (that would break closures entirely), not a frozen snapshot, and not global — it is reachable only through the closure.
options: It is destroyed, so the inner function throws on every call.
It is copied once, so every inner function shares the same snapshot forever.
It stays alive, captured by the closure, and each call sees the latest value.
It becomes a global variable accessible from anywhere.
practiceItems.prompt: A function returns an inner function that increments a variable declared in the outer function. What happens to that variable after the outer function returns?
practiceItems.title: Closure state

practiceItems.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (A, D). Then the microtask queue drains before any macrotask, so the promise callback (C) runs before the timer callback (B), even though the timer was scheduled first. The other orders either run the timer too early or interleave synchronous and async code incorrectly.
options: A, B, C, D
A, D, B, C
A, D, C, B
A, C, D, B
practiceItems.prompt: console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D'); In what order do the letters print?
practiceItems.title: Microtask versus macrotask order

practiceItems.explanation: fetch rejects only on network failure. HTTP statuses, including 404 and 500, resolve normally with a Response, so code must check response.ok or response.status. It does not retry, and it never resolves with null for a completed HTTP response.
options: It rejects with a 404 error.
It resolves with a Response whose ok property is false.
It retries automatically until it succeeds.
It resolves with null.
practiceItems.prompt: A fetch request receives an HTTP 404 response. What does the returned promise do?
practiceItems.title: Fetch and HTTP errors

practiceItems.explanation: Clicks bubble from the target up to ancestors, so a parent listener can inspect event.target and handle every item, including items added later, with a single listener. Clicks do bubble, addEventListener works on any element, and delegated listeners run during bubbling, after the target phase.
options: Because clicks do not bubble, so items cannot handle their own clicks.
Because one parent listener uses bubbling to handle current and future items with less memory.
Because addEventListener only works on container elements.
Because delegated listeners run before the event reaches its target.
practiceItems.prompt: Why attach one click listener to a list element instead of one listener to each list item?
practiceItems.title: Event delegation

practiceItems.explanation: unknown accepts any value but forbids using it until it is narrowed with a check, so mistakes become compile errors. any also accepts everything but disables checking entirely, so errors surface at runtime. never accepts nothing, and object is too broad to use safely without narrowing anyway.
options: any, because it accepts everything
unknown, because it forces narrowing before use
never, because it accepts everything
object, because it covers all JSON values
practiceItems.prompt: A function receives untrusted JSON data. Which type is the safe choice for its parameter?
practiceItems.title: any versus unknown

practiceItems.explanation: React.memo compares props shallowly by reference. A new object literal every render is never referentially equal to the previous one, so memo sees a changed prop and re-renders. React.memo works for function components, accepts object props, and does not require useMemo on the component itself — the fix is a stable reference for that prop.
options: React.memo only works for class components.
The inline object is a new reference on every render, so the shallow prop comparison fails.
React.memo requires all props to be primitives.
The component must also be wrapped in useMemo.
practiceItems.prompt: A component wrapped in React.memo still re-renders on every parent render. Its parent passes an inline object literal as a prop. Why?
practiceItems.title: React.memo defeated by props

practiceItems.prompt: What happens to context consumers when the context value changes?

practiceItems.description: Write a debounce function: it takes a function fn and a delay in milliseconds, and returns a new function that postpones calling fn until the returned function has not been called for delay milliseconds. Only the most recent arguments should be used.
examples: debounced('a'); debounced('b'); — after the delay, fn is called once, with 'b'.
hints: Keep a timer id in a closure and clear it on every call before setting a new timer.
Forward the latest arguments with rest parameters and spread.
practiceItems.title: Implement debounce

practiceItems.description: Write a generic TypeScript function first that takes an array of any element type and returns its first element, or undefined for an empty array. The return type must follow the array's element type.
examples: first([10, 20]) returns 10, typed as number | undefined.
hints: Declare a type parameter T and type the parameter as T[].
Return items[0], whose type is T | undefined under noUncheckedIndexedAccess-free defaults only if you annotate the return type as T | undefined.

practiceItems.description: Write a React custom hook useCounter that takes an initial value (default 0) and returns an object with count, increment, decrement, and reset. Each component using the hook must get independent state.
examples: const { count, increment } = useCounter(5); — count starts at 5 and increment raises it to 6.
hints: Use useState inside the hook; each caller gets its own state automatically.
Use functional updates (setCount(c => c + 1)) so rapid calls do not use stale values.
reset should restore the initial value captured by the hook.
practiceItems.title: A useCounter custom hook

practiceItems.explanation: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks share the same i. The timers run after the loop finishes, by which time i is 3, so each callback prints 3. With let, each iteration would get its own binding and print 0, 1, 2.
options: undefined three times
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print? for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); }
practiceItems.title: var in a loop with setTimeout

practiceItems.explanation: Calling an async function runs its body synchronously until the first await, so 1 and 2 print, then the await suspends f and its continuation becomes a microtask. Synchronous code continues with 4, then the microtask runs 3. Hence 1, 2, 4, 3.
practiceItems.prompt: What is the output order? console.log('1'); async function f() { console.log('2'); await Promise.resolve(); console.log('3'); } f(); console.log('4');
practiceItems.title: Async function ordering

practiceItems.description: A search box fetches results on every keystroke. A user types quickly, an earlier slow request finishes after a later fast one, and the UI shows results for the old query. How do you fix this, and what else should change about the fetching approach?
practiceItems.solution: Cancel the in-flight request when a new query starts, using AbortController with an AbortSignal passed to fetch, and ignore or discard responses that do not match the latest query. Also debounce the input (for example 300 ms) so a request is not fired per keystroke, show a loading state, and handle abort errors separately from real failures so they do not show an error message. For a fuller solution, use a server-state library, which handles cancellation, deduping, and caching.
practiceItems.title: Stale search results

practiceItems.description: A form input's value lives in a single app-wide context, and every keystroke re-renders the entire application, including expensive unrelated components. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix that keeps the code simple.
practiceItems.solution: The input state is shared through one context, and context has no selectors, so every consumer re-renders on every change. The simplest fix is to move the input state down into the form component itself, since nothing else needs it. If some value genuinely must be shared, split the context so fast-changing and rarely changing values live in separate contexts, memoise the provider value, and memoise expensive children so they skip renders when their props are unchanged.
practiceItems.title: Whole app re-renders on every keystroke

practiceItems.description: A team has three nearly identical list components for users, products, and orders, differing only in the item type and how each item renders. They want one component without losing type safety. How should it be typed, and how does the caller use it?
practiceItems.solution: Write a generic component: interface ListProps<T> { items: T[]; renderItem: (item: T) => ReactNode; } and function List<T>({ items, renderItem }: ListProps<T>). At each use site TypeScript infers T from the items prop, so renderItem receives the correct item type and its properties are checked. This replaces three duplicated components with one type-safe one, and callers need no explicit type arguments in the common case.
practiceItems.title: Typing a reusable list component

practiceItems.explanation: Vertical scaling is simple because the architecture does not change, but the biggest available machine is a hard ceiling and the machine is still a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling removes that ceiling at the cost of distribution problems such as state sharing and consistency.
options: It requires rewriting the application for every upgrade.
It has a hard ceiling: a single machine can only get so big, and it remains a single point of failure.
It cannot improve latency for a single user.
It forces all data to be sharded across machines.
practiceItems.prompt: What is the main limitation of vertical scaling compared with horizontal scaling?
practiceItems.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling

practiceItems.explanation: CAP says that during a partition a system can guarantee at most two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. Since partitions happen in real networks, the practical choice is consistency versus availability while partitioned: refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer with possibly stale data to stay available.
options: It must sacrifice partition tolerance and shut down entirely.
It must sacrifice either consistency or availability, but not both.
It must sacrifice durability, losing all recent writes.
It must sacrifice latency, but can keep consistency and availability.
practiceItems.prompt: A distributed store is partitioned: two groups of replicas cannot communicate. According to the CAP theorem, what must it sacrifice?
practiceItems.title: CAP theorem during a partition

practiceItems.explanation: Write-through writes to cache and database together, so the cache cannot serve a value older than the latest write, but each write pays the cost of both stores. Cache-aside can serve stale data between a write and its invalidation, write-behind risks loss if the cache crashes before flushing, and TTL is an expiry mechanism, not a write pattern.
options: Cache-aside, because the application populates the cache on a miss.
Write-through, because every write goes to the cache and the database together.
Write-behind, because writes are flushed to the database asynchronously.
TTL expiry, because entries disappear after a fixed time.
practiceItems.prompt: Which caching pattern guarantees the cache is never stale after a write, at the cost of slower writes?
practiceItems.title: Write-through caching

practiceItems.explanation: At-least-once delivery can redeliver a message after a crash or timeout, so a consumer that is not idempotent would apply the same order or payment twice. Acknowledging before processing would lose messages on crash, global ordering is a separate and expensive property, and in-memory-only storage loses messages on broker restart.
options: Acknowledge each message before processing it.
Be idempotent, so processing a redelivered message twice has the same effect as once.
Process messages strictly in global order.
Store messages in memory only, for speed.
practiceItems.prompt: A queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. What must its consumers do?
practiceItems.title: At-least-once delivery

practiceItems.back: Many requests miss at once when a popular key expires, and all hammer the database. Mitigate by letting one request repopulate the cache while others wait or serve the stale value, staggering TTLs with jitter, or warming the cache before expiry.
practiceItems.front: What is a thundering herd in caching, and how do you mitigate it?
practiceItems.title: Thundering herd

practiceItems.back: Push (fan-out on write) optimises reads with precomputed feeds but is expensive for celebrity posters. Pull (fan-out on read) makes writes cheap but reads expensive when a user follows many accounts. The standard answer is a hybrid: push for ordinary users, a pull path for celebrities.
practiceItems.front: Push vs pull fan-out for a news feed: what does each optimise, and what breaks each?
practiceItems.title: Push vs pull fan-out

practiceItems.back: Single Responsibility: one class, one reason to change. Open/Closed: extend without modifying. Liskov Substitution: subclasses usable wherever the parent is expected. Interface Segregation: small focused interfaces, not one fat one. Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions.
practiceItems.front: State each SOLID principle in one line.
practiceItems.title: SOLID in one line each

practiceItems.description: Design a URL shortener serving 100 million new URLs per month with far more redirects than creations. State your requirements, capacity estimate, short-code strategy, and how you keep redirects fast and analytics from slowing them down.
practiceItems.solution: Clarify: shorten, redirect, optional custom aliases, click counts; out of scope is link expiry unless asked. Estimate: 100M/month is about 40 creations per second on average, and redirects dominate reads, so this is read-heavy. Generate codes either by hashing the long URL (handling collisions) or by encoding a counter id in base62 (guaranteeing uniqueness, needing an available counter service). Keep redirects fast with a cache of short code to long URL in front of a replicated database, since most redirects hit popular links. Keep analytics off the redirect path: enqueue click events and aggregate them asynchronously, so analytics can never slow down or fail a redirect. Name the bottleneck: the counter service or the primary database on writes, and the cache on hot keys.
practiceItems.title: Design a URL shortener

practiceItems.description: Design a parking lot with motorcycle, car, and bus spots, tickets on entry, and payment on exit. State your classes, how spots are claimed concurrently, and how pricing can change without editing parking logic.
practiceItems.solution: Classes: Vehicle (plate, type), ParkingSpot (number, allowed type, parked vehicle), ParkingLot (spot pools per type), Ticket (vehicle, spot, entry time, pricing), and a PricingStrategy interface. Claim a spot atomically: synchronise the check-and-park step so two threads cannot claim the same free spot. On exit, the ticket computes the fee through its PricingStrategy and the spot is freed. Pricing changes by adding a new PricingStrategy implementation (hourly, daily, surge) without touching Vehicle, Spot, or Lot code. Edge cases: full lot (reject with a clear message), wrong vehicle type for a spot, and a ticket presented twice.
practiceItems.title: Design a parking lot

A raw value leaves no matcher on the stack, so Mockito cannot align arguments to matchers and throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException. The fix is to wrap every argument in a matcher, e.g. when(repo.find(anyString(), eq(10))). The other options describe behaviour Mockito does not have.
options: Mockito treats the raw value as eq() automatically and the stub works.
Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException at runtime.
The stub compiles but is silently ignored.
Mockito matches only the first argument and ignores the second.
practiceItems.prompt: What happens when you mix a raw value and an argument matcher in a single Mockito stubbing call, such as when(repo.find(anyString(), 10))?
practiceItems.title: Mixing matchers and raw values

A suite dominated by end-to-end tests is the slow, hard-to-debug ice-cream cone anti-pattern.
options: Mostly end-to-end tests, with a few unit tests at the top.
Equal numbers of unit, integration, and end-to-end tests.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few end-to-end tests.
Only unit tests, because integration tests are never worth their cost.

practiceItems.description: A test suite passes when tests are run individually but sometimes fails when the whole suite runs. One failing test reads the current date, another writes to a shared static map that a later test reads, and a third waits for an async job with Thread.sleep(200). Diagnose each failure source and propose a concrete fix for each, plus the process for handling the flaky tests in the meantime.
practiceItems.solution: All three are classic flakiness sources. (1) The date-dependent test should inject a java.time.Clock and use Clock.fixed in tests, so 'now' is controlled and repeatable. (2) The shared static map is shared mutable state: reset it in @BeforeEach (or remove the static sharing) so no test depends on execution order or another test's leftovers. (3) The Thread.sleep guess should be replaced by awaiting a condition with a timeout (e.g. Awaitility), so the test waits exactly until the async work completes. Process: quarantine the flaky tests so their failures do not block the suite, reproduce each (run the suite repeatedly), fix the root cause, and only then un-quarantine. Do not just delete them, which would silently lose coverage.
practiceItems.title: Diagnosing a flaky test suite

practiceItems.description: A repository test suite passes against the default embedded database in @DataJpaTest, but the same queries fail in production on PostgreSQL. Explain the likely cause, how to reproduce the failure in tests, and what changes to make to the test setup.
practiceItems.solution: The likely cause is a dialect difference: H2 tolerates SQL, types, or functions that PostgreSQL rejects (or vice versa), so the embedded database hides a real failure. Reproduce it by running the repository tests against real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers: add a static @Container PostgreSQLContainer with @ServiceConnection, annotate the test with @Testcontainers, and set @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) on the @DataJpaTest so the container database is actually used instead of being silently replaced by H2. Pin the image tag to a major version (e.g. postgres:16). Keep these container tests focused on database-specific behaviour; the rest of the suite stays at cheaper layers.
practiceItems.title: Tests pass on H2 but fail on PostgreSQL
